excerpt: An innovative method based on the integration of multi-criteria KPIs in conceptual process design phases was developed to address the sus- tainability assessment of emerging OCCS concepts. The KPIs considered are intended to capture the performance of alternative OCCS strategies for four different dimensions of sustainability (Crivellari et al., 2021), namely technological performance, economy, environment and society. The approach is developed starting from that originally developed by (Zanobetti et al., 2023a), including several elements of novelty, in particular concerning the identification of the best design among alter- native technology concepts and the footprinting of sustainability. Fig. 1 schematizes the workflow of the approach developed in the present study.

The final goal of this step (Step 1 in Fig. 1) is the identification of alternative technologies for a possible design of OCCS. To this aim, the definition of the target power system and the design specifications are first required. Then, alternative technologies potentially suitable for the proposed aims shall be defined, also based on indications reported within technical literature. A systematic procedure was developed to define possible techno- logical concepts for CO2 capture processes applicable to OCCS. The checklist below was developed to univocally specify each carbon cap- ture process further considered in the application of the methodology.

In Step 2 of the method (see Fig. 1), the feasibility of the possible OCCS design alternatives defined in Step 1 is assessed, based on the reference process schemes defined, the specification of the main OCCS operating parameters, and mass and energy balances. Process simulation software may be used to model steady-state conditions of OCCS systems (e.g., Aspen Plus). To provide a robust comparison of the sustainability performance, each reference OCCS scheme is simulated considering a convenient CO2 capture efficiency from the inlet exhaust gas as a common reference basis. More specifically, the definition of a benchmark case is necessary at this stage to specify the target for the CO2 capture efficiency. The selection of the OCCS concept having a higher technology readiness level (TRL) as the baseline for benchmarking is recommended. The possibility of integrating fossil fuel-based ship power systems and OCCS schemes in terms of heating and cooling services was ana- lysed. The exploitation of waste heat (e.g., associated with exhaust flue gases from fuel combustion) and the heat sinks available onboard (e.g., provided by low-temperature material streams in LNG-based fuel sys- tems) needs to be maximized to obtain enhanced technological viability of OCCS solutions. Process integration feasibility assessment of OCCS schemes is performed using a specific generalized block flow diagram (BFD) for OCCS retrofit to the power system as a reference. 2.3.5. Evaluation of probable designs Based on the definition of KPIs, an OCCS solution is deemed probable if the corresponding KPI is lower than the alternative concepts consid- ered. Thus, a set including a maximum of four probable design options (namely the best performing per each of the sustainability domains considered in this study) is obtained as the output of Step 3 of the pro- posed method (see Fig. 1). Specifically, less than four probable design options are obtained if a single plausible OCCS alternative scores the best performance within more than one of the sustainability pillars considered. The probable design identification allows therefore to evaluate the most sustainable OCCS design when focusing separately on each sustainability criterion. This is the starting point to identify the best design (see Step 4, Fig. 1), as described in the following.

In the last step of the methodology (Step 4 in Fig. 1), the best OCCS design option is selected based on the assessment of specific aggregated sustainability indices (ASIs). In this study, a two-level approach was developed to quantify the overall sustainability of OCCS. The Level 1 ASI, named overall sustainability index (OSI), defined as in Eq. (13), yields a performance-based ranking of OCCS reference schemes according to different decision-making perspectives introduced to weigh the different sustainability-related aspects considered:

where Wi and NIi represent respectively the weight factor and the nor- malised KPI values for the OCCS scheme of interest, related to the i-th sustainability dimension considered in the study. The values of the NI indices may be calculated by applying an internal KPIs normalisation, considering their corresponding maximum value calculated in the analysis as a reference (Zanobetti et al., 2023a). The Wi coefficients in Eq. (13) represent the relative importance of each sustainability pillar in determining the overall performance level. These coefficients are defined using literature-based approaches, considering different factors, including time (e.g., intergenerational equity), space (e.g., intra- generational equity), and receptor (e.g., human, ecosystem) consider- ations (Dincer et al., 2021; Hacatoglu, 2014). Weight factors may be assigned considering four alternative representative aggregation per- spectives, accounting for the subjectivity of the involved decision-makers in considering multiple sustainability criteria

simultaneously (Crivellari et al., 2021). The weight factors related to the aggregation perspectives considered in the analysis are reported in the Supplementary Material. Alternative normalisation methods and tailored weighing factors may be introduced in the analysis to imple- ment company-specific or site-specific criteria (Pollesch and Dale, 2016). Based on the expression of the OSI aggregated indicator, provided in Eq. (13), the lower its value, the higher the sustainability performance of the OCCS scheme regarding the considered aggregation perspective. A sustainability footprint (SF) was then introduced as a Level 2 ASI. The SF results from the Level 1 OSI values were obtained considering the four different aggregation perspectives introduced in the study. As shown in Fig. 2, the SF is computed as the ratio between the internal surface area of the our OSIs (AreaOCCS) and the overall orthogonal radar chart (AreaCHART). An internal division-by-maximum approach (Norris, 2001) was applied to normalise OSIs on a scale of 0–1. By this procedure, the SF value is always between 0 and 1, and a lower value of SF implies a higher sustainability performance. Alternative probable designs can be ranked based on aggregated sustainability metrics, to univocally identify a single best OCCS design option. The obtained ranking may differ based on the calculated values of multi-criteria KPIs as well as on the weight factors adopted for index aggregation (Zanobetti et al., 2023a). A Hyperion-class cruise ship was considered as a case study for OCCS implementation. This passenger vessel features a 36 MW power system with an expected trip time per year of 6264 h and 10 days per single voyage. A LNG-fuelled lean burn spark ignition (LNG-LBSI) engine was considered as the prime mover, because of its attractiveness for retro- fitting and possible integration opportunities with CO2 capture. Addi- tional technical and geometrical details relevant to the definition and characterization of the main equipment items and streams involved in the reference ship category investigated are reported elsewhere (Ian- naccone et al., 2020). More specifically, the exhaust gas composition referring to a 100% engine load was calculated, as reported in Supple- mentary Material, providing a conservative design approach to OCCS (Feenstra et al., 2019). Such assumption ensures that energy re- quirements for OCCS integration onboard the ship are met throughout the entire sea voyage duration, regardless of the navigation phase considered (e.g., at berth, manoeuvring, etc.) In this study, the captured CO2 was considered to be compressed and totally condensed for cost-effective storage as a liquid, offering the possibility of integrating the conditioning system with the LNG pre- heating facilities. Fig. 3 shows the generalized block flow diagram defined to design the OCCS integrated with the LNG-based power system. In this scheme, the hot exhaust gas deriving from LNG pre-treatment and utilization can be exploited for heat recovery before being sent to the main carbon capture section. Monoethanolamine (MEA) was selected for CO2 separation by chemical absorption, as rec- ommended in the literature (Luo and Wang, 2017). Onboard solvent regeneration allows ship-based carbon capture to operate continuously also with a limited footprint (Feenstra et al., 2019). Concerning the cryogenic capture strategy, the CO2 desublimation-sublimation tech- nology selected is based on the removal of CO2 as a solid frost on the surface of moving cold metallic beads (Font-Palma, 2021). This solution can separate a highly pure dry CO2 stream from the exhaust gases of ship engines (Font-Palma, 2021). A two-stage CO2 separation concept with polymeric membranes was introduced for the reference ship-based application, due to its compactness and energy requirements compara- ble to conventional amine-based processes (Oh et al., 2022). Ultimately, Zeolite 13X was tested as a separating physical adsorbent for a con- ventional post-combustion pressure swing adsorption (PSA) process (Riboldi and Bolland, 2017). The Level 1 OSI was computed for all the probable OCCS design alternatives identified (Table 9), applying the normal- isation and multi-perspective aggregation approach described in Section 2.4. AS-based OCCS resulted in scoring a ca 2.5 times higher OSI value (i. e., lower sustainability performance) compared to A3C when aiming at minimizing impacts on individuals. Indeed, the significant hazard level for onboard human targets greatly contributes to penalize the adoption of amine scrubbing as OCCS technology. A3C, on the contrary, tends to be significantly outperformed when switching to sustainability evalua- tions more prone to environmental preservation (e.g., egalitarian, hierarchist). This can be justified considering the increased global warming contribution related to carbon emissions from A3C operations. Ultimately, even weighing sustainability domains equally, the signifi- cant safety-related impacts tend to dominate the overall sustainability performance of AS, which emerges as the least-performing option. It is possible to conclude that the identification of the most sustainable so- lution for OCCS can be significantly affected by the aggregation perspective adopted.

4.6.1. Alternative decarbonization solutions Different possible OCCS technologies were analysed for onboard implementation. For the sake of clarity, Table 11 summarises the main strengths and limitations of each reference OCCS solution, considering both the findings from the present analysis and information derived from the literature. The analysis of the alternative OCCS systems evidenced that only amine-based and cryogenic-based concepts can be successfully inte- grated with the LNG-based power system considered in the case-study analysed. The present multi-criteria sustainability assessment shows that, while the amine scrubbing (AS) technology results in both a high purity of the captured CO2 and a mature technology, it faces increased safety and operational cost challenges due to the handling of hazardous solvents and higher consumption of raw materials for carbon capture. Conversely, the advanced cryogenic carbon capture (A3C) system shows a lower environmental performance, primarily due to the significant carbon emissions related to electricity consumption, and proved to be more cost-effective and inherently safer than AS. The Level 1 overall sustainability index suggests that the emerging A3C concept may be the best choice for OCCS design in the near future, according to an indi- vidualist perspective prioritising minimized short-term social impacts. However, when considering environmental impacts over the medium to the long term (e.g., from egalitarian and hierarchist perspectives), the analysis indicates that significant technological enhancements of A3C are still needed to achieve a better sustainability performance level than conventional AS. Carbon Recycling Technology Figure 1 shows a conceptual diagram of the blast furnace process using carbon recycling technology. The coke used in the production of 1 ton of molten pig iron (coke ratio) is reduced by injecting the product synthesized from CO2 (carbon neutral reducing agent) from the tuyeres of the blast furnace in the same manner as pulverized coal, which has long been used in blast furnaces. As the reducing agent synthesized from CO2, methane (CH4) was selected in this study. The technology for synthesizing methane from CO2 and hydrogen, which is called methanation, was discovered by Sabatier at the beginning of the 20th century 8). As shown by the chemical reaction equation and heat of reaction expressed by Equation 1, this is an exothermic reaction accompanied by comparatively large heat generation.

Rist Diagram The potential amount of CO2 emission reduction in a blast furnace process using the carbon recycling technology was studied with a Rist diagram 10,11). In a Rist diagram, the heat and mass balance are considered by separating the blast furnace into upper and lower parts by the temperature of the thermal reserve zone TR (temperature at which heat rise and reduction stagnate). A typical example of a Rist diagram is shown in Figure 2, where the horizontal axis shows (O+H2) / (C+H2), the vertical axis shows (O+H2) / Fe and the operational condition of the blast furnace (Rist operating line) is represented by the line RP. Point W shows the reduction equilibrium condition of wüstite-Fe at TR, and point P is a point determined from the heat balance in the lower part of the furnace. Actual operation passes through point R, which is separated from point W by some distance. At this time, GR/GW is defined as shaft efficiency and is used as an index of reduction efficiency, which is determined by the reactivity of the raw materials, the burden distribution, and other factors. Point Yd expresses the reduction amount (direct reduction amount) by the apparent C in the coke. The slope of line RP, (C+H2) / Fe, shows the specific reducing gas volume necessary to produce 1 t of molten pig iron. In this study, the CO2 emission reduction rate of the blast furnace using the carbon recycling technology was evaluated on a conventional Rist diagram, considering operational constraints. The CO2 emission of the blast furnace was calculated from the unit consumption of carbon charged to the blast furnace (specific carbon consumption). Theoretical Flame Temperature in Front of Tuyere In a blast furnace, hot blast is blown into the furnace from the tuyeres, and the reducing agent which is injected at the same time and high temperature coke present in front of the tuyere react with the oxygen in the hot blast to produce a reducing gas. The temperature of the reducing gas after this reaction is called the theoretical flame temperature (TFT) in front of the tuyere and is used as a control index in actual operation. If TFT is too high, a large amount of SiO gas will be generated in the raceway, and may cause high Si in the hot metal, scaffolding on the furnace wall and other trouble 12). On the other hand, if TFT is too low, heat transfer to the molten iron will be insufficient, resulting in a drop in the hot metal temperature. Here, the upper and lower limits of TFT were set at 2300°C and 2000°C, respectively, based on operational actual results. TFT is calculated assuming 100% of the elements C, H, N and O contained in the hot blast, injected reaction agent and coke react to the form of CO, H2 and N2. The temperature of the coke in front of the tuyere was set at 0.75 times TFT following Ramm’s equation 13).

Figure 4 shows the change of the specific carbon consumption reduction ratio, together with the permissible range (upper/lower limits) of TFT, the region where injection of preheating gas is necessary, and direct reduction carbon. Figure 5 shows a similar diagram for hydrogen injection. Basically, specific carbon consumption can be reduced significantly by massive injection of CN methane or hydrogen. It can also be seen that the O2 concentration in the blast needs to be increased to inject more CN methane or hydrogen. Therefore, at the same O2 concentration in the blast, the specific carbon consumption reduction ratio increase as TFT decreases. In addition, preheating gas injection is also necessary in order to maximize the reduction in specific carbon consumption. Introduction The carbonate formations in the Central Luconia province offshore Sarawak, Malaysia generally form prolific gas producing reservoirs. The field being studies is operated by PETRONAS and is located as shown in Figure 1. The field is primarily of platform type carbonate build-up with a single long gas column overlying an aquifer, and the field production started in 1995. GPS surveillance data, measured on the platform over the past 20 years, have clearly shown a number of striking events related to reservoir compaction and seabed subsidence, as a result of the gas production. Currently PETRONAS is planning to use the field for CO2 injection and storage from nearby high CO2 content gas producing fields. It is therefore important to understand the geomechanics-related risks such as subsidence and uneven lateral movement, fault reactivation, and cap rock integrity associated with the long term CO2 storage design strategy. A 4-D coupled reservoir geomechanical study has been conducted to model the pore collapse behavior of the carbonate reservoir in the field, calibrate the model with the field measured data, forecast the long term seabed subsidence and lateral movement, and also to study the risks associated with CO2 injection with long term storage.
Figure 1—Study field location in offshore Sarawak, Malaysia

Methodology In order to better delineate and enumerate the risks of CO2 sequestration, a novel and inclusive workflow (Figure 2) is implemented which includes constructing validated 1-D geomechanical models together with comprehensive laboratory testing programme, incorporating specialized creep tests. The validated 1-D models were combined with structural model and reservoir model to create a field wide 4-D geomechanical model using advanced time-lapsed coupled geomechanical simulations. The finite element simulations coupled with the dynamic reservoir model provided predictions of the caprock seal integrity and fault behavior for the proposed injection scenario by considering shear damage and plastic strains of the seal and faults.
Figure 2—Workflow for 4-D coupled reservoir geomechanical study

1-D Mechanical Earth Model 1-D Mechanical Earth Model (1-D MEM) consists of 3 main components which includes in-situ stresses, rock mechanical properties and pore pressure along the well. It contains all the relevant geomechanics information for any geomechanics-related applications such as wellbore stability analysis, sand production prediction, caprock integrity assessment, fault stability assessment and compaction and subsidence evaluation. Well calibrated 1-D MEMs are essential as a solid foundation for robust geomechanics analyses. Good quality MEM should be able to explain observed drilling experiences with the modelling results. Four validated 1-D MEMs were selected for the 3-D model construction namely X-1, X-2, X-3 and X-4. The selection criteria are mainly based on data availability (sonic log) and log quality. Rock elastic properties were derived based on sonic logs and conversion from dynamic to static elastic properties was conducted to achieve good match with rock mechanics test data. Rock strength properties were derived from in-house correlations of the region. Emphasis is placed on lithology identification whereby different correlations were applied to different lithologies and to match the wellbore stability predictions with the drilling experiences. Poroelastic horizontal strain method was used to predict and capture the variability of horizontal stresses in different lithologies and formation. The minimum horizontal stress magnitude was calibrated against leak-off test (LOT) data while the stress azimuth was inferred from compilation of regional stress map in Sarawak Basin (Tjia, 1994). Stress regime understanding from the region is normal stress regime transitional to strike slip regime near top of carbonate and in the carbonate section. Horizontal

Reservoir fracture constraint In the present method, storage integrity is enforced through a maximum allowable average reservoir pressure, Pr ≤ Pfrac. In practice, fracture initiation is governed by the local wellbore pressure rather than the average reservoir pressure. A more physically representative constraint is Pbh(t) ≤ Pfrac, where Pbh is the flowing bottom-hole injection pressure computed from the radial flow equation (Eq. 5). Because Pbh > Pr, the current formulation is conservative for highly injective reservoirs but may be non-conservative for tighter formations, where large near-well pressure gradients can induce fracture even when the average reservoir pressure remains moderate.

In the present case study, a single injection well is assigned to each pipeline and reservoir. This configuration concentrates the total injection rate into one well, which in some cases leads to elevated bottom-hole pressures (as observed in Figure 8). In realistic CCS developments, injection is typically distributed across multiple wells, allowing total injectivity to be increased while maintaining acceptable wellbore pressures. Incorporating multiple wells would therefore enable the constraint Pbh ≤ Pfrac to be enforced more realistically.

An increase in fluid pressure of the reservoir will generate increased total horizontal stresses and vice-versa for reservoir depletion (Fjaer et al., 2008 and Zoback, 2010). With the increase in pressure of the fluid which is partially supporting the stresses acting on the reservoir rock, the rock wants to expand but it is unable to expand laterally. Hence, there will be an increase in the total horizontal stresses to compensate for the tendency of the rock wanting to expand. As the total horizontal stress change is smaller than the fluid pressure change, the change in the effective horizontal stresses is reverse i.e., increase in the total horizonal stress will be associated with a decrease in the effective horizontal stress. In the case of cooling the reservoir rock, the rock has tendency to contract and hence, there will be a reduction in total horizontal stresses and increase in effective horizontal stresses. The thermal effect is much more pronounced in the reservoir where it is dominated by convective heat flow, whilst it is a much slower process in the caprock with conductive heat flow due to its low permeability. The total horizontal stress change in the reservoir will cause reverse stress change of smaller magnitude in the immediate caprock e.g., total horizontal stress increase in reservoir during injection will give rise to total horizontal stress decrease in the caprock to maintain stress equilibrium (Fig. 1). In addition, the pressure and stress changes, and the CO2-rich brine-rock interaction will alter the mechanical properties as well as petrophysical properties of the rock. Stratigraphy The Perth Basin's sedimentary sequence spans from the Permian through to the Quaternary (Fig. 3). Within the Triassic–Jurassic succession sit the Sabina Formation (averaging 165 m thick) and the Lesueur Sandstone (about 2070 m thick). Geometry. Defining the reservoir boundary conditions is typically the most time-consuming part of building a geomechanical FEM model. Formation surfaces and fault polygons are usually derived from seismic interpretation, which is well suited to constraining stratigraphic and structural models for the area of interest, and an upscaled geological grid can usefully be carried into the geomechanical model. Changes in stress state during CO2 injection could potentially reactivate existing faults and, in turn, cause caprock leakage, so mapping and investigating faults is essential to assessing reservoir and cap-rock stability throughout the injection period. More than 30 faults were mapped across the field (Fig. 11), predominantly

oriented N-S in keeping with regional fault trends. On a Mohr-Coulomb chart, stress states are expressed in terms of SH, Sh and Sv — the maximum, intermediate and minimum principal stresses, respectively — and fault stability is expected to shift as this stress state changes (Wu and Hasegawa., 1996; Ganguli and Sen., 2020; Mortazavi and Maratov, 2024; Mathur et al., 2024). The outer Mohr circle has radius (SH-Sv)/2 and is centred at (SH+Sv)/2, and under the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion, rock failure occurs once this circle touches the failure envelope (Noel et al., 2019; Van den Bogert and Van Eijs., 2020). As pore pressure rises with continued CO2 injection, the reservoir's effective stress magnitudes shift and the calculated Mohr circle moves leftward, directly reflecting the change in the reservoir's stress state (Leclere and Fabbri., 2013; Hedayatzadeh et al., 2022) (Fig. 16).

Stress Charting and Evidence of Rock Failure. The stress-charting technique offers a way to interrogate each simulation iteration's predictions, establishing a stress path that links changes in stress to changes in pore pressure. For every cell in the simulation model, the Mohr circle can be plotted against the failure envelope (Fig. 16): the area enclosed by the blue semi-circle in Fig. 16 tends to expand as pore pressure rises, and would eventually breach the failure envelope, signalling possible formation failure, including fault reactivation. As Fig. 16 shows, however, no such breach of the failure envelope occurred at any timestep or cell location within the Yalgorup or Wonnerup formations over the simulated injection period, indicating no possibility of failure in either formation. The stress-charting process also yields the principal stress magnitudes (SV, SH, Sh) and the Sh and SH orientations for every simulation grid cell, providing useful quality-control information for assessing model performance and supporting the derivation of stress–strain relationships. This result likewise holds for the isothermal case; the Mohr circles shown do not carry the additional thermal contribution to effective stress that would arise in the cooled region near the injection wells.

4.1.2. Petrophysical parameters The relative permeability functions for the initial conditions based on laboratory measurements on core samples and after calibration are shown in Fig. 4. The calibrated relative permeability function does not deviate signiﬁcantly from its initial state during the inversion. Earlier inversions showed signiﬁcant deviations and implausible values in the mixed saturation region. The capability to detect eﬀective ratios be- tween saturated and multiphase permeability is attributed to the si- multaneous inversion of pumping tests and CO2 injection. Single phase hydraulic ﬂow allows a sensitive determination of the intrinsic per- meability, while CO2 injection is additionally sensitive to the relative permeabilities of CO2 and brine. At the Ketzin test site, the CO2 injec- tion pressure buildup is about twice as high compared to the intrinsic formation permeability. As consequence, a skin factor is introduced to the injection well Ktzi201 only for the CO2 migration model. The skin factor is calibrated to a value of 10.1, which is a considerable value. It causes pressure variations about twice as high compared to a well without skin. This results in realistic relative permeability functions. Two processes that are not captured by the current model could increase the CO2 injection pressure while not aﬀecting the intrinsic permeability. Salt precipitation near the injection well, as observed by pulsed neutron-gamma logs (Baumann, 2013), reduces porosity and perme- ability near the wellbore and would reduce the injectivity of CO2. It is, however, a complex and dynamic process and the temporally constant skin factor can only be a ﬁrst approximation to the phenomenon. The primary formations of interest for IBDP are the Ironton-Galesville, Eau Claire Shale, Mt. Simon Sandstone, Pre-Mt. Simon Sandstone unit, and the Precambrian basement (Fig. 1). The Ironton-Galesville is a saline formation and serves as the first monitoring interval above the regionally extensive Eau Claire Shale. The Eau Claire Shale is composed of tight limestone, interbedded shales and siltstones. The Eau Claire is the primary seal for the Mt. Simon Sandstone and is approximately 152 meters (m)/ 499 feet (ft) at the IBDP site. The Mt. Simon Sandstone is a regional blanket sandstone that is the primary target for geologic carbon storage in the Illinois Basin; it is approximately 453 m (1,486 ft) thick [2]. The lower Mt. Simon Sandstone has average interval porosities of 20% and permeability of 185 millidarcy (mD). However, there are low permeability units within the lower Mt. Simon Sandstone with permeabilities <1 mD the most notable of which is the low permeability streak located at approximately 2,092 – 2,094 m (6,863 – 6,870 ft) depth [1]. Prior to injection, it was unknown how these lower permeability units would affect the migration of CO2 in the lower Mt. Simon Sandstone, as they did not appear to be laterally extensive based on the well log data from the project wells. The Mt. Simon Sandstone is underlain by a thin low reservoir quality Pre-Mt. Simon Sandstone unit that has distinct lithology and porosity from the Mt. Simon Sandstone and the Precambrian basement [3]. The diagnostics identified by Strandli and Benson [18] provide a relatively simple means for assessing reservoir structure (heterogeneity in form of layering and anisotropy) and approximate height of the CO2 plume in the absence of formal inversion of the multilevel pressure transient data. In order to allow for easy comparison of the pressure buildups at different depths, the pressure buildup in each monitoring zone is normalized to the pressure buildup in the monitoring zone at the depth of injection. At early time, the depth of injection is where the pressure buildup will be the highest. If the reservoir is highly heterogeneous and/or anisotropic, the shallower monitoring zones will experience less pressure buildup and the normalized pressure buildups will be much less than unity. With time, normalized pressure transients are diagnostic of the height of the CO2 plume, as buoyancy-induced migration of CO2 will give rise to larger pressure buildups at shallower depths, with upward flow of displaced brine above the CO2 plume and downward flow of displaced brine below the plume. There have been studies of different LCO2 storage pressures because it is advantageous to transport CO2 as a liquid for large-scale transport and CO2 cannot be liquefied at atmospheric pressure. Pure CO2 can be liquefied and stored at various pressure conditions between the triple point (5.1 bar, −56.6 ◦C) and the critical point (73.8 bar, 31.1 ◦C) [10, 11]. In particular, previous studies have demonstrated that storage pressures above 25 bar are economically unfeasible when considering the economics of various pressure conditions in the CCS value chain, which includes CO2 liquefaction systems, storage tanks, and CO2 transport ships [11]. The most commonly mentioned storage pressure conditions below 25 bar are 6.5–7.0 bar [10–20] and 15 bar [10–13,17, 21]. At a storage pressure of 6.5 bar, the amount of LCO2 that can be stored per unit volume can be increased by approximately 8.5 % compared to a storage pressure of 15 bar, due to the difference in density [16,17]. Conversely, at a storage pressure of 15 bar, the higher lique­ faction temperature reduces the power consumption required for liquefaction compared to 6.5 bar [10,11]. Table 1 shows that most studies have assumed storage pressures of 6–7 bar and 15 bar.

many studies have been done on the optimal process design for CO2 liquefaction. The required liquefaction temperatures for pure CO2 at storage pressures of 6.5–7 bar and 15 bar are −50.6 to −48.5 ◦C and −27.7 ◦C, respectively [15,17]. Therefore, previous studies have pro­ posed liquefaction processes utilizing single refrigerants such as ammonia, propane, CO2, propylene, and R134-a to meet these lique­ faction temperatures (Table 1). Among these, the liquefaction process using ammonia as a refrigerant has demonstrated the lowest power consumption and is regarded as the most efficient liquefaction process [12,22,23]. However, most of the previous CO2 liquefaction studies focus on CO2 liquefaction, rather than CO2 boil off gas (BOG) re-liquefaction.

To transport LCO2 over long distances by ship, the CO2 BOG re- liquefaction system is essential as part of the cargo handling system (CHS). LCO2 must be stored at temperatures below room temperature, which can lead to BOG problems when transported by ship [24]. CO2 BOG can be managed in three ways: venting it while paying the carbon tax, re-liquefying it or holding it at the expense of increased tank pres­ sure. Venting BOG not only releases greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions but also results in cargo loss. Additionally, when considering the carbon tax, venting may be less economical compared to re-liquefaction. When the voyage is short, allowing the tank pressure to rise may be a practical option. Previous study has shown that the holding time of LCO2 storage tank is approximately 12–13 days when the pressure increases from 6 bar to 8 bar [25]. For longer voyage exceeding this duration, CO2 BOG re-liquefaction becomes essential to maintain operational safety and prevent cargo loss. Previous studies on CO2 BOG re-liquefaction, similar to those on CO2 liquefaction, have proposed re-liquefaction processes using a single refrigerant such as ammonia, propane, or CO2 (Table 1). For liquefied natural gas (LNG)-powered ships, CO2 BOG re-liquefaction using the cold heat of LNG BOG has also been suggested [18].

Fig. 1(a) shows the vapor compression cycle using a single refrig­ erant, which was conventionally used in previous CO2 liquefaction studies [11–13,17,23]. A single refrigerant was compressed in compressor 2 and cooled in cooler 2 by cooling water. After undergoing Joule-Thomson (JT) expansion in valve 2, single refrigerant absorbed heat from the target gas in the heat exchanger and then circulated back to compressor 2. The target gas entered the compressor 1, where it was compressed to high pressure and cooled to a low temperature through heat exchange with the refrigerant in the heat exchanger. It then un­ derwent JT expansion through valve 1 to the pressure of the storage tank, where it was partially liquefied. The liquid separated in the separator flowed into the storage tank and the non-condensable gas was either purged or recycled into the compressor. If the CO2 was pure, all of the separated gas could be recycled back into the compressor. However, if the CO2 contained light impurities, purging was necessary to prevent

Fig. 3 shows the PFDs used in this study. Fig. 3(a) shows the re- liquefaction process with a single refrigerant, ammonia, as a conven­ tional re-liquefaction process. The CO2 BOG was compressed to high pressure through two-stage compression and cooled to a low tempera­ ture through heat exchange with ammonia in a heat exchanger. It was then partially liquefied by JT expansion to the storage pressure through a JT valve and separated into gas and liquid in a separator. The liquid was sent to the storage tank, and the vapor was recycled to the compressor. If the N2 content was high, some vapor needed to be purged to prevent accumulation in the cycle. Fig. 2 presents a graphical illustration of the overall discharge sys­ tem. The interface system between ship and terminal tanks must ensure compatibility between the ship’s LP and the terminal’s MP conditions. The system includes two main transfer lines: (a) the LCO₂ discharging line and (b) the vapor return (VR) line, which is necessary to maintain ship tank pressure. Onboard cargo pumps pressurize the LCO₂ to match the terminal tank pressure, with additional head considered for MP conditions, while onshore heat exchangers (HTX) warm the LCO₂ to terminal saturation temperature before storage. At the same time, onshore coolers condition the vapor returning to the ship to match tank conditions. Onboard VR control valves regulate flow based on the ship’s cargo tank pressure set point. At the terminal tank side, vapor generation during loading must be managed to prevent over-pressurization and ensure stable operation.

During the discharging operation, LCO₂ is transferred from the ship’s cargo tanks to the terminal storage tank via the liquid header, ship’s manifolds, and marine loading arms. Prior to discharging, the ship tanks are filled to 96 % of their volume with LCO₂. The operation concludes when the tanks retain a minimum heel for the ballast voyage, e.g., 4 % volume. The process includes five (5) thermodynamic transitions, as depicted in the phase diagram of pure CO2, Fig. 3:

During the loading of CO₂ from a terminal to a LP ship, the control of temperature and pressure is essential to ensure safe and efficient transfer. The interface system, Fig. 4, includes components for condi­ tioning both the liquid stream and the VR. At the side of the loading line, onshore HTXs are used to cool the liquid CO₂ stream, especially when subcooling is required to minimize vapor generation in the ship tank. Onboard Joule-Thomson (JT) valves depressurize the liquid to match the ship tank pressure, enabling controlled entry into the cargo tanks. At the side of the VR line, onshore VR compressors increase the pressure of the returning vapor to align with terminal conditions. Moreover, onshore HTXs cool the vapor stream to the terminal’s required tem­ perature. Pressure-controlled liquid cargo valves (located either on­ board or onshore) regulate flow and maintain system stability during the transfer.

During the loading operation, LCO₂ is transferred from the terminal tank to the ship’s cargo tanks. Upon arrival at the export terminal, the ship tanks contain the minimum heel, which helps maintain pressure during the ballast voyage. The loading process concludes when the tanks reach 96 % of their volume with LCO₂. Heijungs and Frischknecht (1998) deﬁne Life Cycle Assessment as a “systematic method for evaluating the environmental impacts of a product or system through all stages of its life cycle, from raw material extraction through production, use, and disposal.” This comprehensive approach ensures that environmental impacts are not simply shifted from one stage or category to another. Traditionally, LCA studies have focused on analyzing well- established systems after they have been deﬁned, requiring extensive data on both background and foreground processes, and typically aligning the assessment time in the present (Cucurachi et al., 2018). Notwithstanding the importance of the traditional LCA approach, a prospective element seems to be missing. Anticipating an improvement in system performance may be difﬁcult, at early stages of system design when applying changes is easy; however implementing potential improvements becomes difﬁcult and costly if the need for such change is apparent at later stages of system design (Collingridge, 1982). This dilemma highlights the importance of adopting a strategic approach to capture the environmental implications of technologies during their early development phases by shifting the focus of the LCA study to a more distant future. Prospective LCA addresses this dilemma by intervening in the early growth phases when the technology’s environmental blueprint can still be meaningfully shaped and modelling background system scenarios, for instance, future energy systems (Arvidsson et al., 2018). While emerging technologies often seek to enhance existing functions performed by established technologies, the comparison may not always be straightforward, particularly when emerging technologies possess unique properties. The scarcity of primary data is a notable issue, often representing only lab-scale or pilot- scale conditions, impacting the reliability and relevance of results (Cucurachi et al., 2018). This scarcity extends to both foreground and background processes. To conduct a pLCA, it is necessary to model the system at a future time, when the production scale of the emerging technology under study has increased compared to its current level. Fig. 1 shows the steps required to develop a reservoir model suitable for an MILP optimization problem. The starting point is the availability of simulations from a trusted full-scale reservoir simulation model. These can then be provided as input to the POD-TPWL method, which produces as output a reduced-order model of the reservoir. The latter needs to be fully linearized and formulated as constraints in an MILP problem. The first step to obtain a linear model for CO2 storage using the POD-TPWL approach is to derive simulations from full-scale reservoir simulations; these serve as training set of the POD-TPWL model. (2)) and the multiphase Darcy equation for the phase velocity (Lie, 2016) (Eq. (3)).

The MILP reservoir model is validated by comparing the reservoir pressure computed by the reduced-order model and the full scale model. As a reservoir, we considered a saline aquifer operated with realistic injection values and profiles; additional information on the reservoir properties and modelling details can be found in the Ap- pendix. We note that the proposed model can theoretically be used for any type of underground porous formations; however, we have here developed and tuned the model using a saline aquifer exclusively (which provides the largest CO2 storage availability). Five full-scale simulations of different injections of CO2 into a saline aquifer with six- month timesteps were carried out and used to build the snapshot matrix described in the Methods section. It is important to note that these simulations are independent of the validation simulations discussed later. Of the training simulations, only one was used to derive the Jacobians for the linear model, which can therefore be regarded as the main training simulation. The main full-scale training simulation starts with an injection rate of approximately 2400 tCO2/day, increases monotonically to around 3700 tCO2/day after 2.5 years and remains steady afterwards (see Fig. 2). While we show and benchmark the model along a 5-year period, the training simulations were run with a 30-year period so as to enlarge the pool of snapshots available to the model. The 5-year period was chosen to keep the validation simple and clear.

The linear model’s ability to predict the evolution of the pressure in the well’s cell was evaluated using four additional distinct injection profiles: (i) a scenario starting and ending at the same injection rates as the training data but with a faster ramp-up (min-to-max in 0.5 years), (ii) a scenario remaining within the minimum and maximum injection rates of the training data but fluctuating with a seasonal pattern, (iii) a scenario with a structurally lower injection rate, and (iv) a scenario with a structurally higher injection rate and a faster ramp-up. More information about the scenarios are reported in Table 1.

As shown in Figs. 2 and 3, the linear model demonstrates a good predictive performance, capturing both the absolute value of the (well) pressure and its evolution, with deviations typically within ±5% of the full-scale simulation results for all tested injection profiles. Here, we showcase the integration of the proposed reservoir model into the optimization of the CCS chain using an illustrative case study, where the latter purely serves the purposes of demonstrating how the reservoir model can be used in MILP optimization. The case study considers a typical CCS chain problem: the decarbonization of an industrial cluster comprising a waste-to-energy (WtE) facility and two cement plants that are located onshore at a moderate distance from the offshore reservoir. The case study and its topology are illustrated in Fig. 4. As for the validation, we considered a five-year period with daily resolution for all components excepts the reservoir, which is again modelled with a six-month resolution. We chose a daily resolution because the considered industrial processes have a rather continuous operation, given the nature of their service (waste incineration) or the features of their reactors (high-temperature cement production). Each industrial plant can adopt post-combustion carbon capture (PCC) to avoid CO2 emissions from entering the atmosphere. To incentivize industrial actors to mitigate their emissions, we considered a sce- nario with progressively increasing CO2 tax over time. When PCC is implemented, the captured CO2 is transported via pipeline in the dense (supercritical) phase to a central onshore collection point before injection. Here, CO2 is further pressurized to the required storage conditions, and injected via an offshore pipeline in the saline aquifer. An overview of the main optimization variables is reported in Table 3, and further assumptions underlying the case study are reported in the Supplementary Information. Under the case study’s conditions, the cost-optimal strategy for all point sources in the cluster involves deploying PCC units to mitigate a portion of their emissions. However, the cluster does not achieve full-capacity carbon capture immediately: This delay is attributable to the WtE facility, specifically to the lower CO2 concentration compared to the cement plant, which results in higher operational costs. As a result, when the CO2 tax is lower, it is not cost-efficient to reduce

Indeed, the captured CO2 leads to an optimal average injection rate over six- month timesteps that fluctuates seasonally between 4100 t/day and 3700 t/day (Fig. 5(b)). This average injection rate exhibits a bi-modal trend, reflecting the variability in the emission profile of the cement plants. The resulting injection rate dictates the evolution of the BHP in the reservoir, which increases over time but remains well below the caprock fracture pressure, as ensured by the constraint in Eq. Model portability. The model we present here is, in principle, portable to any MILP optimization framework where it is possible to add user-defined objects. However, two factors need to be taken into account. First, tuning the model to a specific injection site requires having a full-scale reservoir simulator; this should also come with access to the code to extract the Jacobians needed for the linearization process. While this is feasible using open-source software such as MRST (a detailed explanation of how the Jacobians are derived in MRST is provided in the Supplementary Information), it demands familiarity with the principles of full-scale reservoir simulations. Second, the MILP implementation requires the formulation of two distinct time discretiza- tions for different components of the MILP problem, which might not be trivial in existing MILP tools.

The diffusion limit in Eqs. (9) and (10) represents scale-up difficul- ties only with the capacity of the connection, i.e., how much CO2 per year (MtCO2∕year) a pipeline can transport. In building pipelines, the challenge does not stem solely from transport capacity but also, to a substantial extent, from the distance: Longer transport distances require engagement with a larger number of communities and the acquisition of additional rights-of-way for the pipeline corridor. Additionally, the likelihood of crossing a state or country border increases, potentially in- troducing new regulatory hurdles or necessitating bilateral agreements. A purely capacity-dependent diffusion limit, suitable for technologies such as photovoltaics, may not adequately represent the challenges of scaling up pipelines. To address this limitation, the diffusion limit includes the distance by incorporating binary variables that represent pipeline construction.

For this purpose, we introduce two additional versions of the diffu- sion limit. Both versions take the capacity-based diffusion constraint in Eq. (10) as a basis and adapt the knowledge stock equation Eq. (9). One version uses the distance as the sole determinant of the diffusion limit, excluding the pipeline diameter from the constraint. The second version includes the product of capacity and distance, thereby accounting for both aspects of pipeline construction simultaneously. Consequently, pipeline expansion can be constrained in one of three ways: by capacity, based on annual flow (in MtCO2∕year, Eqs. (9) and (10)); by distance (in km, Eqs. (11) and (12)); and by their combination, the capacity- distance (in MtCO2 km∕year, Eqs. (13) and (14)). All three approaches share the same fundamental diffusion parameters: the diffusion rate and the pioneering capacity addition term. The diffusion rate is dimen- sionless and therefore applicable to all formulations. The pioneering capacity addition term differs in magnitude and units to reflect the absolute size of initial installations.

The effect of a favorable environment for scaling up is shown in the sensitivity analysis (Fig. 4). The diffusion parameters significantly influence whether the CO2 network scales up successfully and achieves the climate targets. If diffusion parameters are high (e.g., 𝜗> 20 % and 𝜁> 200 MtCO2 km∕year), pipeline deployment is not the bottleneck for network scale-up. In fact, more than one solution to the scale- up problem is available for policymakers to consider: improving the diffusion speed through targeted regulation, supporting early projects to enable larger pioneering installations, diversifying transport modes, or exploring domestic CO2 storage space. These many options offer opportunities to create favorable conditions for expanding the CCTS infrastructure, while balancing other aspects such as social accep- tance. The presented framework for diffusion parameters provides a systematic tool for quantifying trade-offs among these options.

While algorithmic developments are not the prime focus of this work, we propose a simple heuristic procedure as a first step to address compu­ tational efficiency. Recent reviews provide complementary accounts of SSM progress, CCUS-network modelling, and regional application (Lin et al., 2026; Rahmanta et al., 2026; Table 1). This review addresses a narrower question: how source allocation, shared transport topology and capacity, and operational feasibility are represented jointly in planning models. Its contribution is an explicit evidence framework that distinguishes sequential, jointly optimized, and decomposition- based coordination, and separates demonstrated CCUS results from transferable or prospective AI and digital-twin capabilities. It does not infer a universal method ranking where direct comparative evidence is unavailable. As shown in Figure 3, the spatial mismatch between sources and sinks, together with the need for multi-stakeholder coordination, gives rise to substantial structural complexity in SSM. Rather than being a one-dimensional pairing or route-planning problem, SSM is a combinatorial decision problem in which network topology design, multidimensional constraints, and multi-objective optimization are closely intertwined. This complexity is reflected in three forms of coupling.

SSM research is increasingly moving beyond the optimization of local pilot projects toward cluster-based deployment across regions, national borders, and ultimately global systems. As illustrated in Figure 4, the dominant paradigm is evolving from simple source- sink connections toward networked, clustered, and dynamic configurations (He et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). Early studies predominantly employed point-to-point matching, pairing individual emission sources with storage sites primarily based on geographical proximity and focusing on the minimization of transport distance or system cost (Boavida et al., 2013).

AI-related methods should be distinguished by decision horizon and evidence maturity (Table 3). Mathematical programming remains the principal approach for strategic infrastructure planning because it explicitly represents investment, capacity, flow, and feasibility constraints (Kattel et al., 2026). Existing AI/ ML reviews focus mainly on materials discovery, process prediction, plume forecasting, and broader system-integration possibilities rather than validated source–sink-network control (Mazhar et al., 2026). Learning-based methods could prospectively support repeated operational decisions when a validated simulation or monitoring environment is available, but the reviewed evidence remains component-level or scenario-specific rather than end-to- end large-scale network deployment.

As illustrated in Figure 5, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can formulate repeated allocation or scheduling decisions as a Markov decision process and learn policies through interaction with a specified simulation environment (Sutton and Barto, 1998). In this review, this role is presented as a prospective methodological application rather than as direct evidence of operational CCUS network deployment. Its potential role is therefore operational adaptation, rather than strategic network design. Direct demonstrations for large-scale source–sink–network systems and controlled comparisons with exact optimization remain limited. Claims of DRL advantage should report training cost, inference time, feasibility and constraint-violation rates, robustness to distribution shift, and performance against a strong optimization baseline.

Operating and planned hubs reveal constraints that abstract network models often omit. Porthos combines a shared onshore gathering system with an offshore pipeline and depleted-gas-field storage, illustrating the value of open-access trunk capacity and staged emitter connection (Porthos, 2026). Northern Lights uses ships to aggregate geographically dispersed emitters before transferring them through a subsea pipeline to offshore storage; its phased expansion makes multimodal scheduling and capacity reservation central decisions (Equinor, 2026). In North America, the Summit Carbon Solutions proposal demonstrates that a technically connected network can still be reshaped by permitting, landowner, and routing constraints; the Iowa filing covered approximately 688 miles of 6–24 inch pipeline (Iowa Utilities Commission, 2026). These cases motivate the endogenous treatment of phasing, access rules, multimodal interfaces, and route approval (Table 4).

Transport-mode selection is fundamental to optimizing CO2 transport systems, with economic performance and applicability largely dependent on transport volume, distance, and spatial distribution (Gunawan et al., 2024). Current CCUS transport systems are dominated by pipelines, supplemented by shipping, rail, and road transport, thereby forming a multimodal system suited to diverse application scenarios (Uddin et al., 2025), as illustrated in Figure 7.

CO2 gathering hubs can integrate dispersed emission sources and connect pipelines with rail or shipping to form multimodal transport networks, thereby improving system flexibility while reducing overall transport costs (Hyypiä et al., 2026). In hard-to- abate sectors and cross-regional deployments, multimodal transport and coordinated regional optimization have become important means of enhancing CCUS system resilience (Kattel et al., 2026). Consequently, the reliability of CO 2 transport and storage networks is a direct determinant of the feasibility of net-zero building pathways, as visualized in Fig. 1. A building's net-zero status depends on abating both operational emissions from its energy use and embodied emissions from construction materials such as cement and steel. While CCUS applied to upstream sources such as power plants for electricity and industrial plants for materials enables this abatement, the entire pathway hinges on the consistent performance of the capture, transport, and storage infrastructure. This creates a critical interdependency: un- certainty in pipeline capacity or storage injectivity can reduce CO 2 deliverability and affect the reliability of building-sector decarbon- ization claims. If this infrastructure underperforms, the expected CO 2 reductions may not be achieved, directly affecting the carbon account- ing of net-zero building strategies. Therefore, planning this enabling infrastructure requires a risk-aware framework that explicitly quantifies and mitigates exposure to such deliverability shortfalls.

Fig. 2 presents the comprehensive, three-stage framework developed for risk-aware planning of CO 2 transport and storage infrastructure, which forms the core methodological contribution of this study. The framework is designed to systematically integrate uncertainty into the infrastructure design process, moving from data synthesis through advanced optimization to comparative analysis. The process begins with the data preparation stage, which establishes a harmonized, synthetic dataset to ensure internal consistency for controlled experimentation. This stage involves compiling four cohesive sets of techno-economic parameters. For industrial emission sources, which represent facilities such as cement plants and steel mills that are critical to building material supply chains, key data include annual production, specific emission factors, and the resulting capturable CO 2 volume, paired with associated capture costs. For pipeline corridors, the data encompasses route lengths, nominal transport capacities, and capital and operating costs. For geological storage sinks, the defining parameter is injectivity per well, coupled with site development and well drilling costs. Global system parameters, such as discount rate, project lifetime, and carbon credit profiles, complete the dataset. The use of a synthetic, internally consistent dataset is a deliberate choice to provide a controlled bench- mark for comparing deterministic, robust, and risk-averse formulations under identical network and cost assumptions.

The prepared data feeds into the central mathematical modeling - stage, which employs a shared MILP structure to model the source-sink network. This tiered structure is reflected visually in Fig. 2 by the stacked progression from deterministic to robust to risk-averse models within a single optimization pipeline. The foundational model is a deterministic MILP that identifies the cost-optimal network by selecting discrete pipelines and wells under the assumption that all capacity and injectivity parameters are fixed at their nominal values. Building on this, the Gamma-robust variant introduces a proactive hedge against uncer- tainty. It treats pipeline capacity and well injectivity as parameters that can shrink within a defined band and incorporates a robustness budget. This budget allows the planner to control the degree of conservatism, forcing the design to remain feasible even when multiple components simultaneously degrade toward their worst-case values. The most advanced formulation is the scenario-based CVaR-shortfall model. This model transitions from guaranteeing feasibility to explicitly managing performance risk. It evaluates designs against a set of discrete scenarios representing different realizations of capacity and injectivity. By incor- porating a Conditional Value-at-Risk penalty on the annual storage shortfall into the objective function, the model directly discourages designs that would perform poorly in the worst-case scenarios, thereby allowing the optimizer to trace a cost-risk frontier. This progression from deterministic to robust to risk-averse modeling provides a versatile toolkit for planners with different risk preferences.

The deterministic optimal solution presented in Fig. 5 establishes a reference infrastructure network designed under the assumption of perfect technical performance. This baseline system meets the pre- scribed annual capture target at the lowest net present cost under the assumption of perfect technical performance. While the specific network topology is dependent on the synthetic case study parameters, the broader implication for net-zero building strategies is universally rele- vant. Decarbonization claims for both building operational energy and embodied construction materials fundamentally depend on the premise that captured CO 2 is reliably sequestered annually, not merely on average over time.

Most significantly, the deterministic baseline represents a system highly vulnerable to underperformance. As demonstrated in Fig. 6 through Fig. 9, introducing uncertainty in pipeline capacity or storage injectivity necessitates substantial and discrete investments in addi- tional infrastructure to maintain the same annual capture target. Translated to the context of building sector decarbonization, this reveals that the credibility of a net-zero pathway does not hinge solely on the theoretical availability of CCUS technology, but critically on the engi- neered reliability of the transport and storage infrastructure under realistic deviations from ideal performance assumptions.

The analysis reveals that, under the assumed techno-economic con- ditions and network geography, the credibility of net-zero building pathways is disproportionately vulnerable to uncertainty in geological storage performance compared to transport infrastructure. As shown in Fig. 6, enforcing a worst-case hedge on pipeline capacity alone increases the optimal net present cost by approximately 18% relative to the deterministic baseline. By contrast, hedging against injectivity uncer- tainty alone increases cost by approximately 52%, while hedging against both uncertainties raises cost by approximately 72%. Although case- specific, the ranking identifies which uncertainty most threatens deliv- erable CO 2 storage that underpins operational and embodied mitigation. In the context of this study, which assumes typical pipeline and storage cost structures and a relatively simple geography with shorter transport distances, injectivity uncertainty emerges as the dominant driver of cost escalation. This is because the system must compensate for injectivity risk by adding discrete storage capacity to maintain annual deliver- ability. However, in more complex geographies or constrained permit- ting environments where routing is difficult and transport distances are long, pipeline additions can become disproportionately expensive. Under such conditions, transport-capacity uncertainty may become comparable to, or even exceed, injectivity uncertainty in its impact on total system cost.

If injectivity is lower than expected, each well can store less CO 2 per year, so the only reliable way to maintain an annual capture and storage target is to add storage capacity, most commonly by drilling additional wells. This response is visible in Fig. 8 through the sharp increase in well counts as the injectivity robustness budget in- creases. Because wells and site development are discrete and capital- intensive, storage underperformance translates into a steep cost response and directly threatens annual delivery that underpins net-zero accounting for both operational and embodied emissions.

Pipeline-capacity uncertainty is structured differently and can be more flexible to manage within a network. Transport derates usually create bottlenecks on specific arcs, and the system can often respond by adding parallel lines on those routes. Fig. 9 shows that pipeline kilo- meters can increase substantially as the pipeline-capacity robustness budget rises. However, under the assumed cost structure and relatively short transport distances, those additions increase total net present cost less than the storage-side expansions required under injectivity uncer- tainty, as reflected in Fig. 6. Fig. 7 reinforces the same interpretation: cost increases more rapidly with injectivity hedging than with pipeline- capacity hedging, and the ridges in the contour surface indicate threshold effects where a small increase in conservatism triggers an integer jump in wells or pipes. Under conditions similar to those assumed here, the results support early emphasis on storage-side char- acterization and contingency capacity, while noting that long distances, routing constraints, and difficult terrain can shift cost sensitivity toward transport.

Fig. 11 through Fig. 13 explain how this reliability is purchased in infrastructure terms. Fig. 11 shows step-like reductions in mean annual shortfall as risk aversion increases, indicating that risk reduction is driven mainly by discrete changes in build decisions rather than gradual operational tuning. Figs. 12 and 13 show the corresponding step in- creases in wells and pipeline length. The planning implication is that tightening reliability requirements can trigger discontinuous capital expansions. For net-zero building strategies, this supports staged deployment and contingency design, such as pre-permitting additional well pads, securing sink expansion options, and protecting transport corridors for upgrades, because modest changes in reliability targets can require the next capacity block.

A primary implication is that infrastructure reliability can be treated as a measurable and enforceable performance standard. The cost-risk frontier in Fig. 10 provides a direct mechanism for operationalizing this principle by quantifying the investment premium required to reduce exposure to severe shortfalls. Policymakers can use this relationship to define and justify reliability criteria for infrastructure approval and carbon-crediting programs, and to differentiate between average ex- pected abatement and delivery-assured abatement that supports durable net-zero building claims.

The analysis also indicates that reliability improvements often require discrete, non-marginal capital expansions rather than incre- mental tuning. The stepwise capacity changes in Fig. 9, Fig. 12, and Fig. 13 indicate that modest changes in performance standards, risk tolerance, or technical assessments can trigger threshold increases in required investment and permitting scope. Net-zero building strategies that depend on CCUS therefore benefit from adaptive, phased deploy- ment plans that anticipate these breakpoints, including pre-permitted sink expansion options, secured pipeline corridors that preserve up- grade feasibility, and monitoring protocols linked to predefined con- tingency actions.

The techno-economic assessment of and potential for CCS from CHP plants in Sweden is based on a set of models, as illustrated in Fig. 1. A process model provides the CHP steam cycle performance when driving an MEA-based CO2 absorption unit, for a set of CHP plant case studies. The energy demands of the capture plant are calculated using the carbon capture plant model of Ignell and Johansson (2021). The modeled process performances are used as inputs to the DH system unit commitment model, which assesses the impact on CHP plant operating patterns of integrating carbon capture, including full-load hours and carbon capture potential. The unit commitment analysis is applied to all CHP plants in Sweden (biomass and waste-fired) in their respective local DH system contexts, based on a CHP plant database. Finally, applying the process and system model results, an estimation is made of the capital and operational expenditures of carbon capture, as well as the costs for CO2 truck transport to an intermediate storage hub, in prepa­ ration for onward ship transport and final storage. Based on the cost estimates, a marginal abatement cost curve for CHP plants with CCS is developed. The following subsections describe the Swedish CHP plant portfolio, the modeling methods applied, and the economic assumptions made in relation to the cost estimations.

The CHP plant database contains information on all the Swedish CHP plants that combust biomass or waste (110 plants in total), located in 78 geographically distributed local DH systems. The data encompass nominal CHP plant heat and electricity production capacities, flue gas condenser installations, live steam conditions and year of commis­ sioning. Fig. 2 presents the distributions of steam cycle power-to-heat ratios, thermal capacity, and fuel type for all the plants in the data­ base. The fuel is here divided into biomass (typically residues from the forest industry) and waste, (municipal solid waste, a certain fraction of which is fossil-based in the form of plastics). The thermal capacities of the boilers range from 7 MW to 540 MW, and the steam cycles have power-to-heat ratios in the range of 0.1–0.65. Thus, there is a wide va­ riety of plant types with differing designs, examples of which are given in Section 2.2. Although it may seem obvious that the application of CCS in the smaller plants (with capacities down to around 10 MW included in this study) will be associated with higher costs, all the plants are included so as to assess the entire cost range for CCS. Details of the database are available in the Supplementary Material.

Steady-state process models of CHP plants are developed in Ebsilon Professional and simulate the impact on steam cycle performance of the integration of amine-based, post-combustion carbon capture. In total, 14 steam cycle designs with different fuel types, live steam conditions, and power-to-heat ratios are considered to represent the range of CHP plants in the database. Fig. 3 gives a schematic overview of the steam cycle designs modeled, where steam extractions A–C are optional and used to cover the range of performances of the considered plants. The included steam extractions and the corresponding pressures for each plant modeled are given in Table 1, together with the live steam temperatures and pressures. The steam turbine isentropic efficiency is set to 88%, independent of case. The boiler is represented in the model by a steam generator component, with a boiler efficiency of 90%, and with fuel

composition specified according to Table 2. In practice, the fuel composition and moisture content vary depending on, for example, the biomass type, although this aspect is neglected in this study. The biogenic share of the waste is assumed to be 52% (Statistics Sweden, 2019). DH is generated in the backpressure condenser, and where applicable, also in an extraction condenser and/or a flue gas condenser. Boundary conditions for the DH water are set to 50◦C for the inlet temperature to the backpressure DH condenser and 90◦C for the supply temperature. Prior to entering the carbon capture plant, the flue gas undergoes flue gas cleaning and is cooled in a flue gas condenser (FGC), which contributes to DH generation. At the time of the present study, 85 of the 110 plants in the database have flue gas condensers installed. An FGC is assumed to be installed at plants that are not already equipped with one, together with the retrofit of the carbon capture plant. The steam cycle models are simulated in design mode without car­ bon capture as a reference case, and in off-design mode with a 90% carbon capture rate. The off-design simulation takes into account steam turbine part-load performance based on Stodola’s law (Cooke, 1985) and calculates the (reduction in) turbine stage pressure when steam is extracted to the reboiler. The boiler load is kept constant in the reference and carbon capture cases, and the changes in electricity and DH outputs are simulated. In addition to electricity and DH, some plants deliver steam to industrial processes (not shown in Fig. 3), and the delivery of process heat is maintained when CCS is integrated.

2.4.3. Local CO2 transport cost Once captured, compressed, and liquefied, the CO2 is transported from the CHP plant to an intermediate storage hub, from where it is subsequently transported by ship to a permanent storage site (Fig. 4). The transport of CO2 between the plant and the hub is assumed to be by truck, since all CHP plants have access to the road network infrastruc­ ture. Train transport could be a feasible option for CHP plants located in cities with access to the railway network, although it would not neces­ sarily be cost-competitive compared to truck transport for sites with small volumes of CO2 to transport (Kujanp¨a¨a and Pursiheimo, 2017). Pipeline transport is not the most likely option in Sweden, due to the lack of an existing large-scale pipe grid, potential problems with public acceptance, and a rock-ground that makes the building of (underground) pipelines expensive (Kj¨arstad et al., 2016). The present work considers seven intermediate storage hubs that have coastal locations (Table 5). Four of these are industrial sites with considerable CO2 emissions that have been identified by Kj¨arstad et al. (2016) as possible hub locations. The remaining hubs are cities in re­ gions with a high population density, i.e., there are several large CHP

plants located nearby from which CO2 could be collected. The truck transport cost is calculated using the parameters listed in Table 6. The cost includes vehicle investments, fuel, labor and mainte­ nance. Eqs. (3)–(6) present an overview of the calculations. The number of trucks required, Ntrucks, is dimensioned based on the volume of CO2 captured during 1 day of full-load operation (YCO2,day) and the volume of CO2 transported per day per truck, YCO2,day,truck, which is a function of the distance traveled, L, and vehicle speed, v. Truck drivers are assumed to work 8-hour shifts (tshift), with three shifts per day (Nshifts,day). Drivers work 5 days per week, resulting in the need for 5 drivers per truck. The fuel cost is calculated based on the number of trips per day (with full- load operation, Ntrips,day) and the driving distance per trip. The cost of the drivers’ wages and fuel costs are multiplied by the plant capacity factor, to account for seasonally varying operation. The maintenance cost is calculated as 5% of the investment cost.

However, the practical feasibility of these results should be studied in greater detail with regards to part-load operation and turbine retrofits. Off-design simulations of part-load operation indicate that some plants might experience problems with reduced pressure in the turbine stage in which the reboiler steam is extracted, i.e., a steam pressure lower than the 3 bar needed to drive the reboiler. Part-load operation might, therefore, require either: (i) that less steam is extracted for CCS so that the steam pressure increases to a sufficient level, thereby yielding a lower capture rate; (ii) that steam is extracted at a higher pressure; or (iii) that an auxiliary boiler is used to provide steam to the reboiler. A CCS value chain comprises several elements within an upstream boundary at one or multiple stationary emitters of CO2 and the down- stream boundary at the ﬁnal sink, which could be one or multiple CO2 storage sites. This paper considers the CCS chain’s conditioning, trans- port, intermediate storage, and injection and geological storage ele- ments, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . The capture of CO2 consists of all technologies and chemical pro- cesses used to separate CO2 before or after combustion processes and those chemical processes with an output stream gas composed mainly of CO2 (e.g., fermentation of biomass). The conditioning element com- prises the compression or liquefaction of CO2 , aiming to increase its den- sity for eﬃcient transportation. The CO2 conditioning element is linked to the transport mode adopted. If transported by pipelines, CO2 can be compressed to higher pressures than 7.3 MPa (i.e., dense phase ﬂuid). If batch-wise transportation is adopted (i.e., using ships, lorries or trains),

The conditioning element of the CCS chain aims to increase the den- sity of the CO2 stream to enable adequate transportation ( Aspelund and Jordal, 2007 ). The conditioning method relates to the transport option adopted downstream of the chain. CO2 may be compressed above its critical point ( > 7.39 MPa) for pipeline transportation into a dense phase ﬂuid. However, for batch-wise ship transportation, the CO2 is expected to be cooled and pressurised to just above the triple point (− 56.5 °C, 0.5 MPa) ( Paul et al., 2012 ). Following the ISO 14,040 norm in deﬁning the goal and scope, this analysis aims to provide accurate GHG footprint estimates from the batch-wise transportation of CO2 using ships and lorries as input for the MILP models developed in this research, so that both CCS chain cost and GHG emissions are considered in the optimisation. The outcomes envisaged in this prospective study are important for stakeholders and developers, as most of the optimisation models for CCS chains do not ac- count for batch-wise transportation and the related GHG emissions are not considered when assessing the whole CCS chain development. Thus, it could provide relevant information for large-scale deployment of CCS chains, particularly in regions where batch-wise transportation plays a signiﬁcant role (i.e., in Europe). The product system of batch-wise trans- portation of CO2 includes liquefying CO2 , intermediate storage, loading, ship or lorry transportation, and oﬄoading of liqueﬁed CO2 . These ele- ments form the product system boundary, comprising the construction and operation phases for a thirty year long time horizon. Instead of a typical functional unit that ought to be focused on the system product, this study uses a reference unit set as 1 t of CO2 transported as the key reference ﬂow in this gate-to-gate study. The selected impact category for this study is the global warming potential (GWP), and the LCIA methodology used is that of midpoints from CML 2016 with GWP 100 years ( Universiteit Leiden, 2016 ). Life cycle inventory model for CO2 liquefaction The transportation of CO2 requires liquefaction to increase its den- sity, which can be achieved through cooling and pressurising just above its triple point. Both main processes for cooling CO2 (i.e., internal and external cooling loops) have electricity consumption as a crucial parameter for modelling, as are documented in previous studies by Roussanaly et al.
