LCI model for intermediate storage facility construction Buﬀer storage using storage tanks is necessary to manage the inter- mittent nature of batch-wise transportation, enabling the cycle of CO2 capture and ship loading, unloading while maintaining consistent pres- sure and temperature during the injection into the geological storage reservoir. The size and capacity of these tanks may vary depending on the facility, batch-wise transport capacity, and desired level of security for the buﬀer concerning ship roundtrip ﬂexibility. Storage tanks may be situated close to CO2 stationary emitters and also close to the storage hub, which can consolidate multiple streams of CO2 captured from sta- tionary emitters, or receive liquid CO2 from various ship routes, jointly or separately with nearby stationary emitters connected to the hub via pipeline for conditioning and further injection. The LCI modelling approach devised for this element of the CCS chain considers two distinct contributions to the intermediate storage facility GHG emissions accounting, one from the inventory model for storage tanks and another from the intermediate storage facility con- struction. The facility storage tanks can be spherical, vertical, or horizontal cylindrical. The beneﬁt of spherical tanks over the other two types is a thinner wall thickness required and a lower heat transfer surface. The vertical cylindrical reduces the land footprint required compared to the horizontal option, thus is recommended when there is no height limit. For this LCI model, vertical cylindrical tanks are considered for two pres- sure conﬁgurations (i.e., 7 and 1.5 MPa). Ship construction. There are many designs of CO2 transport ships, but none are currently operating in the CCS chain. The use of ships for food- grade CO2 exists and is widely spread but for smaller volumes than the ones required for the CCS chain. Also, there are diﬀerences and im- plications on the pressure design of those ships regarding their trans- port capacity and capacity to carry other products such as LPG. The inventory model devised in this research considers two existing life cycle Inventories for the ship construction and adds to these the CO2 storage tank inventory. Our prospective LCA study distinguishes two system boundaries: System boundary T, including only the transport step, and system boundary T+C, including, additionally, the conditioning steps for trans- port and storage (Fig. 1). Furthermore, we distinguish between batch- wise and pipeline transport. Batch-wise transport includes both the transport of the full CO2 vessel to the sink and the transport of the empty vessel back to the source, while pipeline transport only includes the one-way transport of CO2.

System boundary T neglects conditioning to focus solely on the transport step. Hence, environmental impacts for system boundary T are independent of the CO2 source and sink. System boundary T serves the function to transport conditioned CO2 from the capture plant to the sink, with a functional unit of 1 ton of conditioned CO2 transported over 1 km (= 1 tkm). CO2 enters and leaves the system boundary T at defined conditions, either in the gaseous, liquid, or dense phase, depen- dent on the transport mode. The transport steps differ for batch-wise and pipeline transport (Fig. 1).

Fig. 1. System boundary for (a) batch-wise CO2 transport and (b) CO2 pipeline transport. In (b), the transport conditioning step is divided into two parts based on the pressure of the pipeline inlet and outlet. The pressure increase from pipeline outlet to inlet pressure is required to overcome the pressure loss in the pipeline and is thus allocated to system boundary T.

For on- and offshore pipeline transport, we consider transport in both gaseous and dense phases. We assume a pipeline length of 200 kilometers and a mass-flow rate of 0.3 and 10 Mt CO2 per year. To derive inventories, we determine pipeline configurations using the optimization algorithm of Oeuvray et al. (2024) and follow the method- ology of ecoinvent for natural gas pipelines. The pipeline optimization algorithm determines the pipeline configuration with the lowest lev- elized cost for transporting CO2 for a specified CO2 mass-flow rate and pipeline length. The pipeline configuration includes the inner and outer pipeline diameter, the inlet pressure, the number of recompression stations, and the electricity demand for recompression. The optimized inlet pressure of the pipeline can vary between 15 and 30 bar for gas pipelines and 80 and 350 bar for dense pipelines. Thus, the inlet pressure can substantially exceed the outlet pressure of 15 bar for gas pipelines and 80 bar for dense pipelines. While system boundary T+C considers the full transport conditioning, system boundary T only considers the pressurization that is required to overcome the pressure loss in the pipeline (Fig. 1, bottom). Thus, we slightly modify the optimization algorithm to allocate the CO2 pressurization between the conditioning and transport step (Supplementary Material A).

The steel demand for pipeline construction is derived from the pipe geometry. Similarly, the demand for coating materials for corrosion protection is estimated based on the pipe geometry, assuming the same coating material and thickness as in ecoinvent’s natural gas pipelines. Pipelines are assumed to be operated at ambient temperatures of 15 ◦C for onshore and 4 ◦C for offshore pipelines and, thus, do not require any insulation material (Oeuvray et al., 2024). Sand demand for the burial of the onshore pipelines is calculated based on trench geometry recom- mendations (Bahadori, 2017; Koen et al., 2012). Additional inventory data is taken from ecoinvent’s natural gas pipelines and linearly scaled with the pipeline cross-section area. In 2020, the climate impacts can already be very low with 4 gCO2-eq. per tkm for pipelines (Fig. 2). The impacts are low primarily due to two factors: First, there are few greenhouse gas emissions from the operation, with low electricity requirements for repressurizing of CO2 at recompression stations, and second, the large transport volume of pipelines over the lifetime results in low specific impacts from construction.

(1) Electricity- or e-fuels-based transport modes undergo a sub- stantial reduction in climate change impact between 2020 and 2035 regardless of the IAM scenario (Supplementary Material Figure A.10 and A.11), due to the decarbonization of electricity with minor differ- ences in decarbonization speed between scenarios. The climate change impact reduction rate is closely linked to the electricity demand of each transport mode, with higher relative reductions observed for modes with greater reliance on electricity. The climate change im- pacts of electric trains and trucks fall well below the impact of diesel barges and diesel trucks, which are competitive today only due to the high-greenhouse gas electricity grid mix. Similarly, the climate change impacts of methanol- and ammonia-fueled ships are initially higher than those of heavy fuel oil ships due to the greenhouse gas intensity of the electricity for electrolysis. However, impacts of both methanol and ammonia-fueled ships quickly fall well below the impacts of con- ventional heavy fuel oil ships for a decarbonized energy system. After 2035, climate change impacts continue to fall slowly for all electricity or e-fuels-based transport modes due to the falling greenhouse gas footprint of steel, cement, and some carbon-based fuels.

(2) Transport modes using diesel-like fuels, such as trucks and barges, have high initial climate change impacts that steadily decline to comparable levels with trains and electric trucks in the scenarios SSP2- NDC and SSP2-PkBudg500 towards 2100. The decline of climate change impact is due to an assumed increasing share of biofuels and e-fuels. Without the decarbonization of the diesel market mix in the pessimistic scenario SSP2-Base, the climate change impact of diesel-based transport remains high (Supplementary Material Figure A.11).

METHOD AND DATA High-precision evaluations of geological structures, techno- economic factors, and carbon-neutrality targets are crucial steps toward achieving large-scale deployment of carbon geological storage and achieving neutrality goals. However, there is currently a scarcity of publicly available assessment reports on site selection and storage capacity for CO2 geological storage at the sub-basin and zone scales. This is particularly true for zone- scale assessments and studies on onshore/offshore storage capacities in China. Through data compilation and algorithm development, we propose a high-resolution framework for site selection, hierarchical capacities, economic analysis, and source- sink pairing. This involves a multiple-stage assessment integrating technical scheme definition, suitability, algorithms, data compilation, and data-driven analysis at ∼1 × 1 km2 grid resolution (Shown in Figure 3). Unlike traditional meter-to-hundred-meter-resolution single-reservoir models, our kilometer-gridded system enables national-scale CCS infra- structure planning by identifying strategic storage hubs and optimizing cross-basin source-sink pairings. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Utilizing the database and evaluation framework, the CO2 sources, site suitability, hierarchical capacities, techno-economic features, and source-sink pairing of CO2 streams with onshore and offshore aquifer sites were assessed. 3.1. CO2 Emission in Coal-Based Energy and Industry in China Sector-specific data sets were systematically compiled from China’s coal-fired power plants, crude steel production facilities, cement manufacturing units, and coal chemical industries in 2022. The integrated database encompasses geographic locations, production capacities, actual outputs, key industrial processes, and resource consumption patterns (including fuel, water, steam, and electricity) across these energy-intensive sectors. The inventory of CO2 emissions from coal-intensive sectors in this evaluation is presented in Table 2.

CO2 emissions from coal-fired power plants were obtained from the China Electricity Council (CEC), calculated based on annual electricity generation and technology-specific emission factors (e.g., ultrasupercritical and supercritical units). Human activities continue to push greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions closer to critical Earth system tipping points, exacerbating the climate crisis [1]. The IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report underscores that only immediate and profound reductions in emissions can mitigate cata­ strophic climate impacts [2]. Recent data (Fig. 1) indicate that fossil fuel and industrial CO2 emissions reached an all-time high of 36.3 Gt in 2024 – a 0.9 % year-over-year increase [3]. Concurrently, global mean surface temperatures for 2011–2020 were 1.1 ◦C above pre-industrial levels (1850–1900) [4]. This accelerated warming is driving unprecedented glacier retreat, sea-level rise, and extreme weather frequency, threat­ ening global ecosystem stability and socioeconomic security [5]. Consequently, addressing emissions from major industrial point sources (e.g., cement kilns, coal-fired power plants, and petroleum refineries) has become a critical scientific and technological challenge for stabi­ lizing global temperatures [6–8].

As an integrated technological approach, carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) aims to establish a complete carbon management chain from emission sources to geological storage, thereby preventing industrial carbon emissions from entering the atmosphere [9–11]. The core of this technological system lies in the precise coupling of three key stages (Fig. 2): source capture (efficiently separating and concentrating point source CO2 using technologies such as oxy-fuel combustion and post-combustion capture) [12–14], safe transportation (enabling large-scale carbon transport through high-pressure pipeline networks, cryogenic vessels, or regional hubs) [15–17], and permanent storage (injecting supercritical CO2 into depleted oil/gas reservoirs, deep saline aquifers, or basalt formations, achieving geological isolation over mil­ lennium timescales through physical trapping and mineralization re­ actions) [18–20]. Climate modeling studies consistently identify CCUS as an indispensable technological pillar for achieving the Paris Agree­ ment’s 1.5 ◦C target. Model projections clearly demonstrate that emis­ sion reduction scenarios without CCUS fail to stabilize atmospheric

CCUS projects have undergone commercial deployment worldwide (Fig. 3) [22–24]. Several major economies including China, the US, the EU, Australia, and Japan have implemented storage verification projects across various scales [25,26]. Global verified geological CO2 storage data in 2023 show that the US (8061.812 Gt), China (3077.431 Gt), and Australia (502.43 Gt) rank top three, collectively accounting for 89.8 % [27]. Other countries advance industrialization through divergent technical pathways: Pioneering the world’s first industrial-scale cross-border CO2 storage solution, Norway’s Northern Lights initiative utilizes depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs in the North Sea’s Sleipner area. This hub offers 1.5 million tons of annual storage capacity, con­ necting major German and French industrial emitters through maritime transport of liquefied CO2 [28]. Japan conducts a large-scale subsea bed storage demonstration in Tomakomai, verifying the feasibility of storage in pyroclastic rock formations [29]. Canada’s Boundary Dam power station has significantly reduced carbon capture costs by implementing post-combustion capture technology [30].

Although substantial breakthroughs have been achieved in techno- economic analyses of individual technical components, systematic re­ views of cross-regional, multi-factor synergistic source-sink matching mechanisms remain scarce. This study focuses on the core issues in this field by establishing a three-dimensional “source-sink-matching” analytical framework to systematically synthesize recent global ad­ vances in source-sink matching research. As illustrated in Fig. 4, our research encompasses key technical aspects, including the spatiotem­ poral characteristics of CO2 emission sources, assessment of geological storage capacity alongside site selection criteria, transport modes, and multi-scale matching models, and conducts hierarchical analysis of existing literature across four scales: global, national, regional, and in­ dustrial. Through hierarchical analysis and critical synthesis of existing literature, this study thoroughly examines four core issues: synergy bottlenecks in techno-economic policies, data accuracy and scale mismatch, limitations in transport and matching mechanisms, and intelligent algorithms and data-driven approaches. These findings pro­ vide crucial support for enhancing the theoretical foundations of CCUS source-sink matching systems and optimizing integrated carbon man­ agement solutions, offering new impetus for scaling CCUS deployment and advancing global carbon neutrality.

Globally, while diverse screening criteria exist across regions due to variations in geological basement characteristics and development stages, they universally adhere to a comprehensive evaluation framework with geological integrity as the foundation, engineering adaptability as the support, risk early-warning mechanisms as safeguards, and socioeconomic acceptance as boundaries [76]. The table categorizes key screening parameters into four primary dimensions: geophysical prop­ erties, engineering parameters, risk assessment, and socioeconomic factors. Under geophysical properties, critical sub-indicators such as caprock integrity, reservoir configuration, permeability ratios, and pore structure directly determine CO2 containment security and storage ef­ ficiency. Engineering parameters—including injection rate, volume, and wellbore integrity—constrain operational feasibility, while risk and so­ cioeconomic elements such as seismic hazards, leakage potential, public perception, and regulatory policies reflect external uncertainties and social acceptability. This multidimensional framework enables a holistic assessment that balances technical potential with practical deploy­ ability, providing a standardized yet adaptable tool for preliminary site selection across diverse geological and regional contexts.

CO2 geological sinks refer to technological systems that actively inject atmospheric CO2 into subsurface formations through natural processes or engineered interventions [135,136]. Core pathways include mineral carbonation reactions [137], karst carbon sink effects [138], and oceanic dissolution absorption [139], along with deep geological storage—the most scalable mitigation approach—permanently seques­ tering CO2 in supercritical state (>31.1 ◦C, >7.8 MPa) within saline formations, depleted reservoirs, or deep strata beyond 800 m depth [140,141]. As shown in Fig. 11, current global CGS and utilization technologies exhibit tiered development: CO2 storage coupled with in-situ uranium leaching (CO2-ILU) has achieved commercial applica­ tion, where China, Russia, USA, and Kazakhstan inject CO2 into sand­ stone uranium deposits, dissolving uranium oxides (UO2 2+) in acidic conditions, significantly enhancing uranium recovery while concur­ rently storing CO2 [142]. CO2-EOR technology has entered commercial implementation phase, operating by injecting supercritical CO2 into reservoirs to reduce crude viscosity and swell oil phase volume [143,

144]. When injection pressure surpasses minimum miscibility pressure (MMP), CO2 and crude oil form miscible displacement fronts, substan­ tially improving oil recovery (typically by 8–15 %) while enabling structural and dissolution trapping [145–147]. As depicted in Fig. 12, the integrated CO2-EOR process incorporates both external and internal carbon cycles. The external cycle utilizes CO2 captured from industrial sources, which is transported and injected into oil reservoirs to enhance recovery, while the internal cycle involves reprocessing and reinjecting CO2 separated from produced oil and gas. This closed-loop system re­ duces reliance on external CO2 and improves storage efficiency, with a portion of CO2 permanently trapped. Zhang et al. [148] supported its feasibility through a techno-economic model based on six oilfield blocks, showing a break-even oil price of $29.4/barrel with carbon tax and $25.6/barrel without, alongside a 54.7 % emission reduction, confirm­ ing both economic and environmental benefits.

As a critical component of the CCUS chain, CO2 transport mode se­ lection directly impacts project economics and risk profiles [163,164]. Primary transport modes include pipelines, shipping vessels, and tanker trucks (Table 5). Pipeline transport dominates large-scale, long-distance scenarios [165–167]. Analysis of four Germany-to-Norway cross-sea transport scenarios reveals transport cost share decreases from 22 % to 10 % as annual capture volume increases; shipping proves more economical at small scales while pipelines excel at large scales, though scale economies must be balanced against capital lock-in effects [168]. This cost differential stems from pipeline transportation’s economies of scale. China’s multi-sector shared pipeline model indicates 19,000 km of trunk pipelines will be needed by 2050 to support 174 million tons/year carbon capture, with 50 % reused from existing oil/gas corridors [169]. However, pipeline transport must overcome supercritical phase control challenges. Jiao et al. [170] demonstrated that implementing dense-phase transport in downstream supercritical pipelines enhances CO2 storage by 3.4 % through pressure/temperature control coefficients, confirming that transport constraints significantly impact source-sink matching optimization. Furthermore, as Fig. 13 shows, offshore inte­ grated CCS value chains require emphasis on pipeline design, network optimization, phase-change control, and corrosion prevention [171].

Tanker truck transport serves as a supplementary solution for small- scale scenarios, primarily for temporary deployment or pilot projects. Its core challenges lie in pressure vessel safety and long-term transport economics [174]. Although composite materials can reduce vessel rupture risks, per-unit transport costs increase nonlinearly with dis­ tance, making it difficult to adapt to long-distance, continuous transport demands difficult [175]. Current research indicates its role in large-scale CCUS deployment is confined to such specialized contexts.

This paper systematically reviews the entire technical pathway of CCUS source-sink matching, revealing that its large-scale development still faces four interrelated systemic constraints (Fig. 17). First, there are multi-level disconnections within the technology-economy-policy sys­ tem; simplified cost estimation, lack of precision in policy incentives, and barriers to cross-sectoral coupling impede commercialization. Sec­ ond, insufficient data accuracy and scale mismatch between carbon sources and sinks lead to deviations between matching results and actual demands. Third, rigid methods for transport network optimization and insufficient cluster collaboration limit the system’s flexibility and eco­ nomic viability. Fourth, the disconnection between intelligent algo­ rithms and physical mechanisms, coupled with the lack of dynamic evolution characterization, makes it difficult to support precision opti­ mization in complex scenarios. These challenges are intertwined and collectively constitute the core obstacles to source-sink matching.

We conceptualize a planetary limit for geologic carbon storage in the context of harm prevention and risk avoidance. When carbon stor- age is understood as a consumable and depletable common good, transgressing this limit results in permanent trade-offs with other dimensions of sustainable development such as human health and biodiversity27. Future impacts of climate change, their potential revers- ibility and respective consequences will be critically dependent on this limit. We perform a spatially explicit analysis, identifying and syste­ matically applying multiple exclusion layers based on preventa- tive risk analysis to a global map of sedimentary basins suitable for carbon storage (Methods, Supplementary Figs. 1–6 and Supple- mentary Tables 1–3, including for assessed sensitivities). We then estimate a planetary limit for geologic carbon storage by assessing the remaining onshore and offshore basin volumes that meet all risk criteria (Fig. 1).

Policy risk These environmental considerations and perceived risks, as well as general concerns about delaying the scale-up of renewables and the perception that CCS may prolong the use of fossil fuels, have been linked to low levels of public and political support of geologic carbon storage35,36. For example, CCS is currently banned or majorly restricted in some European countries (see Supplementary Table 4 for current countries with restrictive CCS policies), but there are growing discus- sions to adjust the existing regulations to allow onshore and offshore storage to achieve climate targets. However, these policy developments remain politically contested, highlighting the volatile and uncertain nature of public and political support of geologic carbon storage. Recognizing that geologic carbon storage may be a limited resource requires careful consideration to be taken by nation states when devel- oping domestic energy transition and climate plans. Given the millen- nial timescales for which carbon storage is needed to counteract the impact of released CO2 on climate change, decisions made on carbon management today will affect the human population for more than ten generations into the future. This raises the question of which countries, sectors and generations should be entitled to utilize available geologic storage resources. There is unequal impact on countries’ geologic carbon-storage reserves across dimensions of both capabilities to mitigate and his- toric responsibility for emissions based on our analysis (Fig. 4a). Some high-gross-domestic-product countries with high historic emissions such as Russia, USA and Canada are better placed to implement geo- logic storage solutions, whereas other relatively rich historic emitters such as the European region have substantially reduced storage poten- tial. At the same time, some developing countries with robust storage potential such as Indonesia and Brazil, and some countries in Africa, have historically contributed little to global emissions and thus may have weak domestic incentive to exploit their storage resources unless the removals can be traded. In a future that significantly exploits avail- able storage resources, our results indicate that large-scale transfers of captured carbon may occur, resulting in higher risks for leakage

during transmission, either through shipping or via pipelines, and raising question of distributive justice and equity. We also find that oil-producing nations in the Arabian Peninsula, who have the know-how to pursue carbon storage also have storage reserves that are largely robust to our risk-prevention analysis. Other countries with a long history of an active domestic oil and gas industry and also relatively large storage potential include USA, Australia and Canada. For global policy limiting warming to well below 2 °C to be successful, these incumbent industry actors must be appropriately incentivized to become net injectors, rather than extractors, of subsurface carbon. Pre-existing norms in international climate agreements, such as the polluter-pays principle, provide avenues for establishing needed financial frameworks. Even with well-designed policies and markets that incentivize such a reversal in business models, large-scale industries situated in storage-rich nations can develop financial flows in the billions to tril- lions of dollars per year, which could enhance inequality between and within nations54. Still, opportunities exist to enable growth in removing carbon from the atmosphere and storing it today based on principles of fairness, responsibility and respective capabilities. For example, countries with large sovereign funds based on oil and gas revenues could set aside a small portion of their valuations to support the nascent CDR industry55. Next, we briefly describe the type and reasoning for applying each exclusion layer. A summary of each layer’s global impact on our estima- tion of a planetary limit is described in Supplementary Table 1, including a central, lower and upper sensitivity estimate (‘Consistent storage assumptions across spatial scales and sensitivities’). Because each operation is computationally expensive, we apply exclusion layers sequentially. Thus, each estimate of volume removal is dependent on the previous layer applied. If each layer was applied only to the global technical potential, it would by definition exclude a larger volume than we estimated in our sequential application.

Protected-area exclusion layer. The first exclusion layer we apply is the policy based protected areas74. In this exclusion layer, we included areas that have the designation of protected areas as defined by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and the Convention on Biological Diversity. A comprehensive open-source dataset cataloguing the geospatial spread of the protected sites is developed under a joint project between International Union for Conservation of Nature and the United Nations Environmental Program. The database is entitled ‘World Database on Protected Areas’, which comprised 293,692 protected sites in May 2024 (Supplementary Fig. 1a). We overlayed this exclusion mask on our global dataset comprising onshore and offshore sedimentary deposit boundaries to demarcate sedimentary deposit areas outside of the protected zones.

EEZ exclusion layer. The second layer we apply is the global EEZs. The offshore territorial claim of a country is governed by the United Nations Convention on Law of the Sea. The conventions allow for 3 boundaries on the territorial claims of a country: (1) territorial sea, up to 12 nauti- cal miles from the coastline; (2) contiguous zone, up to 24 nautical miles from the coastline; and (3) EEZ, up to 200 nautical miles from the coastline. Within the EEZ, the coastal state has sovereign rights of exploration, exploitation and management of natural resources in both the waters themselves and the seabed below. States have rights regarding the protection and preservation of the marine environment in their EEZ, as well as the construction, opera- tion and use of installations and structures at sea. In this study, we assumed that the maximum country-specific area attributable towards offshore sedimentary deposit will be within the boundaries of coun- try’s EEZ. Any offshore sedimentary deposit area outside of the EEZ will be considered international waters, hence unavailable for explo- ration and construction of deep-sea carbon injection infrastructure (Supplementary Fig. 1b). To mitigate the issues arising from overlap- ping claims over EEZ of a neighbouring coastal state, we have removed the EEZ area75 where overlapping claims or a joint regime is present (Supplementary Fig. 1c,d).

Polar-circle exclusion layer. The third layer we apply is the area within polar circles. Polar circles, namely, the Arctic and Antarctic circles demarcate the global circles of latitude at 66.5° N and 66.5° S, respec- tively (Supplementary Fig. 1e). In our study, we assume that the sedi- mentary basins north of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle do not contribute to the CO2 storage potentials. This assumption is partly derived from the point of view of preserving polar ecosystems that are already sequestering large amount of CO2 and partly owing to the intra-annual climatic and land-cover inaccessibility and associated increased costs of CO2 storage.

for example, close to plate subduction areas, are less suitable for CO2 storage owing to compromise of sealing units or the reactivation of existing faults during CO2 injection31. The reactivation of existing fault structures in areas under far field stress poses a risk for leakage and for failure of these fault structures, potentially leading to low-intensity earthquakes. While in the hydrocarbon sector these geohazards are well understood, there remains uncertainty for the stability of geologic structures for the injections of reactive CO2-rich water (for example, ref. 76). Future use of saline aquifers will therefore force future com- promise between the risk of failure of seals that could cause leakage of CO2. To approximate future choices to mitigate the risk of leakage, we assume that areas of moderate seismic hazard would be avoided. To incorporate such an exclusion zone, we use the global map of seismic hazard77 to exclude areas that have a more than 10% of chance of peak ground acceleration breaching 0.115 g and 0.401 g (moderate in the US Geological Survey Instrumental Intensity scale78) in the next 50 years (Supplementary Fig. 2).

Population-and-human-health exclusion layer. Population centres have a crucial role in site suitability of carbon capture and storage facilities and form the basis of our next exclusion layer. Owing to the potential for toxicity mobilization, underground utility services pro- vision, supply of fresh water, extensive human-made modifications to the topsoil and densely developed neighbourhoods preclude the global site suitability of carbon capture and storage facilities79. We utilize high-resolution datasets of built-up urban areas under different future population and urbanization scenarios80 and choose our exclu- sion layer based on the urban area boundaries in 2100 based on Shared Socioeconomic Pathways narrative 5 (SSP5) entitled ‘fossil-fuelled development’ that incorporates high reliance on fossil fuels and CCS for future global growth81. In our central case, we assume a 25-km dis- tance buffer around the urban boundary to account for a safety margin around the urban conglomerations. A sensitivity for this layer is also conducted by assuming a 5-km buffer zone to account for a less restric- tive policy regime. Global maps of both the central case and sensitivity case, as well as a zoom-in to the Cairo metropolitan region is shown in Supplementary Fig. 3.

Ocean-depth exclusion layer. Here we assess exclusions related to the ocean-depth or water-depth boundary above the offshore basins. The offshore storage of CO2 is advantageous as there is a very low risk of damage to infrastructure owing to induced earthquakes generated from the overpressure within the reservoir. Pumping in shallow seas will be relatively feasible, whereas in deep water the costs will increase. In the pre-salt basins offshore Brazil, drilling for hydrocarbons has been achieved down to water depths of 2,000 m (ref. 82). At the same time, some of the most environmentally damaging events in the history of oil and gas extraction have occurred due to extraction at depth, such as the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which occurred at 1,500 m ocean depth in the Gulf of Mexico and was exacerbated owing to issues of reaching the well head83. Storage-depth exclusion layer. Here we investigate the upper and lower cut-off for storage depth within the sedimentary deposit basins. Storage of CO2 is ideally suited in aquifers below 800 m depth, beyond which the overpressure compresses the gas, its density decreases rapidly and CO2 reaches a supercritical state, maximizing the storage volumes. Assuming a geothermal gradient of 25 °C km−1 and 15 °C surface temperature, the CO2 takes about 30-times less volume compared with surface conditions. Starting at 1.5 km depth, the density and occupied volume stay constant at about 36-times less volume com- pared with surface conditions89. On the basis of the sedimentary depth map for both onshore and offshore sedimentary basins, we estimate a mean depth of 1.9 km for onshore and 2.5 km for offshore basins for a 1 decimal degree global spatial areal grid (Supplementary Fig. 5a). A relatively small number of areal grid cells are present beyond 5 km sedimentary depth. Current literature (Supplementary Table 3) bound minimum and maximum estimates at 800 m and 4 km, respectively. We therefore apply a conservative depth requirement (minimum) of 1,000 m as a global mask to the database of sedimentary basins for our central case. In many ways, in comparison to federal environmental statutes, state law, and particularly state common law, has the potential to provide non-federal actors more comprehensive relief from harm related to the long-term storage of CO2, but also is at risk of preemption by any forthcoming federal regulatory framework on CCS. Unlike the federal environmental statutes, which either do not give states or private parties the right to seek monetary recovery or, in the case of CERCLA, allow only for recovery of response costs, the state common law claims are available to private parties, local governments, and states to recover for a fuller range of harms associated with leakage from stored CO2. Potential claims of trespass, negligence, nuisance, and strict liability, along with potential damages, offer the possibility for compensatory and punitive damages and injunctive relief not available under most federal and state environmental statutes [13]. For CCS, augmenting statutory and common law liability within a tailored regulatory structure is a crucial component of risk management. Opening of Drava and Sava depressions is associated with the con­ tinental rifting that began in Ottnangian age and the main extension stage lasted until Badenian age (Luˇci´c et al., 2001). Two primary methods manage source-sink relationships: full redi­ rection (Fig. 1a) and partial redirection (Fig. 1b). Full redirection transfers all emissions from a full storage site to the nearest available sink, while partial redirection only redirects selected sources, keeping others at the initial site. Unlike full redirection, partial redirection al­ lows splitting emission hubs, offering greater flexibility in balancing storage use, particularly in regions with uneven source-sink distributions.

Clustering sources within a 100 km (Fig. 3a) radius minimizes total system costs by up to 25 % compared to dispersed storage strategies. Full redirection is more cost-effective in Kazakhstan than partial redirection since most CO2 storage sinks have large capacities but are far from emission sources, except in the western region, where sources and sinks are closely aligned (Fig. A1, Appendix). In partial redirection (Fig. A1b), emissions are distributed across multiple sinks, allowing some sources to remain at their initial sites, increasing flexibility but potentially raising transport costs. Developing CCS hubs with multiple emitters enhances cost efficiency in Kazakhstan (Khoyashov et al., 2024). The cost breakdown highlights capture costs as the dominant expense, accounting for 50.47 % of total costs at a 100 km radius, but decreasing to 36.17 % at 180 km due to the increasing contribution of transportation costs (Fig. 4). This shift suggests that as transport dis­ tances increase, pipeline infrastructure and compression costs can be the primary cost drivers rather than capture expenses. Transport costs do not increase linearly but stabilize, suggesting economies of scale in pipeline routing efficiency.

The integration of existing pipeline infrastructure significantly re­ duces transportation costs by leveraging pre-established routes. Fig. 5 illustrates that considering existing pipelines lowers transport costs across all clustering radii, with the most substantial savings occurring in mid-range clustering distances. For instance, at 100 km clustering, transportation costs drop from 11 MUSD to 10 MUSD, while at 400 km clustering, the reduction is from 24 MUSD to 23 MUSD. This cost miti­ gation effect underscores the importance of reusing existing pipeline infrastructure wherever feasible to optimize CCS deployment costs.

Net CO2 abatement rises to about 123 Mt by a 200 km clustering radius and then plateaus because most large emitters are already captured, and the extra energy for longer pipelines offsets the small additional volumes (Fig. 6). Extending the network beyond 200 km, therefore, raises costs without meaningful environmental benefit, making ~200 km the pragmatic limit.

The environmental footprint of CCS hubs is dominated by CO2 cap­ ture emissions, which contribute 99.95 % of total system emissions across all clustering radii (Fig. 6). Properly managed CO2 storage sites have leakage rates below 0.01 % per year, ensuring long-term containment. Potential risks include wellbore integrity failures and caprock permeability, which can be mitigated through continuous pressure monitoring and injection control. Figure 3b illustrates a system block diagram of a ship-based CCS chain. In this study, the range of ship transport was limited to from the liquefaction system to the injection system. Ship transport can be divided into four modules: the liquefaction system, storage tank, CO2 ship, and injection system. The captured CO2 at the capture system is liquefied by the liquefaction system. The liquefied CO2 is preserved in the temporary storage tank until the CO2 ship comes for loading. The stored CO2 is unloaded into the CO2 ship, and the CO2 ship navigates to the offshore storage site. Finally, the CO2 is injected into the storage well by the injection system. Because a high-pressure carrier is more expensive than a low-temperature carrier, the CO2 in the cargo tank of the CO2 carrier was assumed to be in a dense liquid phase. A pressure and temperature of 7 bar and −50 °C, respectively, which are near the triple point, were selected as the liquefaction point. Liquefied CO2 takes up about 1/500 of the volume of gaseous CO2, so CO2 should be liquefied for economical transportation. Because CO2 can be liquefied between the triple point (5.18 bar, −56.5 °C) and critical point (73.8 bar, 31.1 °C), a single point should be determined. The BOG is generated due to the heat ingress into the low- temperature cargo containment system from the surrounding air and seawater. The BOG rate is directly proportional to the heat transfer rate from the surroundings to the cargo. The heat transfer rate largely depends on the heat transfer coefﬁcient and heat trans- fer area as well as the temperature difference. Precise estimation of the BOG rate requires detailed information on the carrier such as the hull dimension, equipment arrangement, cargo tanks, insu- lation, environmental conditions, and voyage conditions. Because such information is not accessible for the moment, this study esti- mates a BOG rate based on the following reasoning. The simplest form of the cargo containment system is shown in Fig. 1. The whole cargo containment system is insulated by the polyurethane form (PUF) on the inner hull plate. To be on the con- servative side for the heat transfer rate, the temperature on the inner hull is assumed to be equal to the stored cargo temperature. Consequently, the heat transfer rate is controlled by the thickness of the insulation layer.

The concept of P-graph is brieﬂy explained in this section. P- graph is a bipartite graph for umabiguous representation of pro- cessing networks. There are two types of vertices: horizontal bars representing operating units; and solid circles representing mate- rial or energy streams; vertices are connected by directed arcs [32]. A simple conventional and P-graph representation of an operating unit (e.g. a gas turbine) is shown in Fig. 2. There are several combinatorial instruments associated with P- graphs [46]. First, the axioms and theorems are to ensure repre- sentation unabiguity and consistencies of the resulting super- structures and solution networks. The other instruments are the three main algorithms which include superstructure construction. Maximal structure generation (MSG) ﬁrst determines an overall structure for the problem which encompasses all possible solu- tions. Next, solution-structure generation (SSG) enables multiple candidate solutions to be identiﬁed as subsets of the maximal structure. Finally, superstructure optimisation is achieved via accel- erated branch and bound (ABB) to identify the best solution among the various candidates based on speciﬁed criterion [45,46]. It should be noted that ABB allows for a more efﬁcient search of so- lution topologies than is possible with conventional branch-and- bound solvers used for MILP models; thus, in the case of large problems, it is possible to achieve signiﬁcant reductions in solution time. Also, the P-graph approach is also able to identify near-

optimal solutions (in addition to the global optimum), a feature which is not possible using other mathematical optimisation techniques, but which may prove valuable for practical decision- making. By comparison, the MILP approach will yield the global optimum, but will not be able to identify comparable solutions. To represent carbon capture options for power plants (i.e. ﬁrst part of the superstructure in Fig. 1) on P-graph, the following steps are needed:
Firstly, the streams involved in this superstructure were iden- tiﬁed as power generated and the power generation cost, as listed in Table 1. Each power plant generates power at different capacity

with a speciﬁc cost; therefore power and cost are the input streams in P-graph. When a carbon capture technique is chosen, the power output after retroﬁt, power loss and compensatory power are then determined, as well as its associated costs due to retroﬁt and compensatory power. These are intermediate streams in P-graph representation. The ﬁnal outputs in P-graph representation are the total power output from all power plants (including compensatory plants), and the overall cost from all plants. In P-graph, operating units are capable of transforming certain materials or streams into other ones in order to produce desired products from the speciﬁed raw materials through the deﬁned in- termediates [43]. In the second step, any possible candidate oper- ating units are listed, as shown in Table 2. All candidate operating units feature different performance and overall costs. Therefore, in the third step, these will be speciﬁed for the solver to choose the optimal operating units based on the objective. The performance of the units is speciﬁed by the amounts of outputs per unit of chosen inputs; while overall costs of operating units are related to the operating costs and investment costs. In this case, the performance of each unit is given in Section 4 and the overall costs are deﬁned by the CO2 emitted by the operating units. Finally, the upper and lower bounds for all streams and oper- ating units are speciﬁed. The limitation is usually depending on the operating unit capacities or availability of resources. This step is important for the solver to choose optimal units and streams to be used, starting with the most proﬁtable and efﬁcient options [43]. For this case, the lower bounds for power plants i for all technology used are the respective initial output capacities.

The 3-stage closed-cycle ( Fig. 3 ), presented by Engel and Kather ( Engel and Kather, 2018 ), is a refrigeration machine that cools and liq- ueﬁes CO2 using a refrigerant. The refrigerant is compressed in the R-C1 compressor to the liquefaction pressure associated with the temperature of the hot source (cooling water). The pressures of the second and the third stages are determined by the liquefaction temperature of the dif- ferent CO2 expander T3 and T4 respectively. For each stage, cooling water is used to chill compressed gas before entering in ﬂash (R-F1 and R-F2). Flash generates saturated liquid used for the CO2 liquefaction. In the presence of impurities, the phase change temperature along the heat exchanger must be considered the outlet temperature of the pinch in the exchanger. The vapor is superheated before entering the compressor to prevent any liquid carryover into it. A ﬂash unit is placed at the end of the chain to treat impurities in the liquid CO2 . Turbines are employed to generate electricity during the expansion of CO2 . The open cycle ( Fig. 4 ) uses the Joule-Thompson coeﬃcient of CO2 for self-refrigeration. Exergy is deﬁned as the maximum useful work obtainable when a system interacts with a reference environment. It characterizes the qual- ity of energy within a system and serves as a valuable metric for quanti- fying ineﬃciencies and losses. In this study, exergy analysis is conducted following the principles outlined by Szargut ( Szargut, 1989 ). The analysis begins with deﬁning the system boundaries, which en- compass all relevant components involved in CO2 transport facilities. This approach ensures that all signiﬁcant factors impacting the exergy performance are considered. The exergy ( Eq. (11) ) of each stream within the system is calcu- lated using the fundamental thermodynamic relationships, taking into account physical and chemical exergy terms, while neglecting kinetic and potential exergy terms. These calculations are performed relative to a reference environment (P0 (1 atm) and T0 (25 °C) with relative hu- midity of 70 %), established to determine the exergy values of the system components under standard environmental conditions. The reference environment proposed by Rivero & Garﬁas ( Rivero and Garﬁas, 2006 ) is considered to calculate the chemical exergy of the diﬀerent molecules.

The electricity source used in the liquefaction process is a crucial fac- tor in the context of reducing the overall carbon footprint of the CCUS chain. The choice of electricity source directly inﬂuences the global emissions associated with the liquefaction process. When electricity is generated from fossil fuels, the associated emissions can signiﬁcantly reduce the overall eﬀectiveness of CO2 capture and storage eﬀorts as show in studies ( Costa et al., 2024b ). Moreover, the transition to greener electricity can support the achievement of net- zero emission targets by ensuring that the process of capturing and stor- ing CO2 does not inadvertently contribute to the problem it aims to solve. Reference scenario In 2020 the infrastructure is still limited since only few pilot sites will be operational. By 2030 the emission reduction targets are sufficiently severe that CCS needs to be developed on a large scale in all countries and in all source clusters considered. As a result, infrastructure requirements are much more extensive (Figure 1). Most of the countries in North-west Europe are able to store their captured CO2 nationally. Some cross-border transport is required, from Belgium to the Netherlands and from Poland to Germany. The Baltic States, Sweden, Finland,

Romania and Hungary lack (sufficient) domestic storage capacity, which results in transport to neighbouring countries. Volumes to be transported are limited, with the largest volume from the Ruhr area and the Brandenburg area in Germany (both almost 50 Mt/yr). The requirements in 2050 (Figure 2) are similar, except that the volumes to be transported are higher, with the largest volume again from the Ruhr area (almost 250 Mt/yr). Furthermore, in contrast to 2030, Poland and the Baltic states now have sufficient national storage capacity due to vast amounts of aquifer capacity becoming available. This is the result of characterizing large parts of their domestic saline aquifer storage reservoirs before that time. Offshore-only and EOR scenarios The infrastructure of the two alternative scenarios is similar since the offshore oil fields are located close to the offshore gas fields and saline aquifers. Both are, however, different from the reference scenario since onshore transport corridors form a large network transporting CO2 towards the North Sea. Due to accumulation of CO2 in the pipelines all the way from Bulgaria to the coast in Germany, large amounts of CO2 leave Germany, heading for the North Sea. Volumes to be transported are up to ~750 Mt/yr in 2050. While such volumes are not realistic, these results illustrate the effect of stringent regulations for onshore CO2 storage.

The results of the source – sink matching show that a large effort in the construction of infrastructure is required between 2020 and 2030 since many additional transport corridors emerge. After 2030 the effort is large due to the construction of parallel pipelines along existing corridors. (The maximum amount to be transported per pipeline (48") is ~70 Mt/yr (150 barg) onshore and ~100Mt/yr (200 barg) offshore. Volumes to be transported well exceed such limits.) Assuming that all transport will occur by pipeline, in 2050 a total amount of ~22.000 km and ~33.000 km of pipeline needs to be in place for the reference and the two alternative scenarios respectively (Table 3). A rough calculation shows that on average ~50-100 km of pipeline per month needs to be constructed, during the period 2020 – 2050. Current pipeline projects have a similar construction pace, so these rates are not uncommon. The Northstream and Nabucco projects, involving pipeline construction for natural gas from Russia to Germany through the Baltic Sea (1200 km) and from Turkey to Austria through Bulgaria, Romania and Hungary (3300 km) are examples of such projects. For these projects, the ime required between start of the planning and end of construction is in the order of 10 to 15 years.

Cross-border transport of CO2 is foreseen to take place on a significant scale as early as 2030. In the reference scenario this is already 25% of the total amount of CO2 captured, while about 70% is to be transported across borders in the offshore-only and EOR scenarios (Table 3). This implies that viable legal frameworks for cross- border transport need to be in place soon on EU and national levels. Apart from the legal level, compatibility must be present at the technical level, to ensure cost-effective linking of national systems. Cross-border transport in the reference scenario is caused by insufficient national storage capacity. The additional cross-border transport in the two alternative scenarios is caused by the lack of offshore storage options in most countries.

The scenario implies a reduction of CO2 emissions from the power sector to 150 Mt/y by 2050, compared to 1423 Mt/y in 2005. The results shown in Section 3.2 include a number of ‘oversized’ pipelines: pipelines which, in anticipation of future ﬂows of CO2, are built with a larger capacity than what is strictly needed at the time of construction. This requires very long planning horizons and implies that governments and/or industry take a volume risk, because future ﬂows may never actually materialise. One way to account for such uncertainty is to increase the discount rate. In this appendix we therefore rerun the simulations with a 15% discount rate, i.e. twice as high as the original 7.5% discount rate used throughout the paper. The characteristics of the resulting optimised network are shown in Fig. 8. It is interesting to compare Fig. 8 with Fig. 7. First of all, the resulting total network length when using a 15% discount rate is greater than when a 7.5% discount rate is used for optimisation. This is a fairly intuitive result: with higher discount rates, there will be less anticipation of future CO2 ﬂows, hence fewer bulk pipelines are built upfront. As a consequence, more pipelines need to be built later on, resulting in greater total network length. Likewise, when a higher discount rate is used, investments in the ﬁrst time steps are slightly smaller, but the total cumulative investment is larger: the difference is 0.9 billion euros in Case 1 and 0.8 billion euros in Case 2. This is also reﬂected in the cost per tonne of CO2 transported, which is signif- icantly lower in the beginning but 0.1 EUR/t higher by 2050 when the higher discount rate is used. All in all, however, the changes seem relatively small, hinting that the characteristics of the opti- mal CO2 transport network are fairly robust vis-à-vis changes in the discount rate assumed for the optimisation algorithm.

Our reference scenario simulates the cost-optimal deploy- ment of a European CCTS infrastructure for the period 2010–2050 given a CO2 certificate price starting at e15 in 2010 and rising to e75 in 2050. CCTS infras- tructure gradually ramps up from 2020 to 2040 (see Fig. 3). At first, the industrial facilities with low capturing costs sit- uated close to potential storage sites are the predominant users of CCTS. Industrial CCTS penetration reaches satura- tion with a capturing rate of 370 Mt CO2 per year in 2050. With rising CO2 prices, CCTS becomes a more attractive abatement option for the power sector. Trapping mechanisms can be divided into primary and secondary processes (Table 2). When carbon dioxide is injected in the subsurface, it is ﬁrst trapped by primary trapping mechanisms (which are static) and hydrodynamic trapping below the cap rock in deep saline aquifers (Bachu et al., 2007). The secondary processes – solubility, mineral and residual trapping – are much slower and occur over a much longer timeframe than the primary mechanisms (of the order of centuries to millennia). The contribution of these secondary trapping mechanisms is almost negligible during the injection phase of carbon dioxide geological storage but they contribute to increasing storage security in the longer term (Bachu, 2008).

Trapping mechanisms can be also distinguished in terms of physical and geochemical processes (Table 2). Over time, the contribution of each trapping mechanism changes. Initially, physical trapping is the dominant mechanism for retaining carbon dioxide in aquifers. As carbon dioxide migrates through aquifers, residual gas and solubility trapping tend to be signiﬁcant mechanisms. These secondary trapping mechanisms enhance storage security because the risk of leakage of the products of such trapping mechanisms does not depend directly on the integrity of the cap rock on which physical trapping depends (Suekane et al., 2008).

4. ECONOMICS OF CARBON DIOXIDE STORAGE IN SALINE FORMATIONS This section considers one of the three CCS component costs – storage cost. Costs for the various components of a CCS system vary widely, depending on the reference plant (whether coal- or gas-ﬁred, hydrogen and ammonia production, gas processing or other industrial sources) and the wide range of carbon dioxide source, transport and storage situations. The cost of employing a full CCS system is dominated by the cost of capture, which is 15–75 US$/tCO2 net captured for a coal- or gas-ﬁred power plant. Typical costs for transportation are in the range 1–8 US$/ tCO2 transported; geological storage ranges from 0.5 to 8 US$/ tCO2 net injected, plus 0.1–0.3 US$/tCO2 injected for monitoring and veriﬁcation (see Table 4).

The storage cost varies for different storage options. The IPCC (2005) presented a compilation of three comprehensive assessments of carbon dioxide storage cost estimates for the USA, Australia and Europe. Table 5 presents estimates from those three studies and shows that representative estimates of the cost for storage in saline formations typically fall between 0.5 and 7.7 US$/tCO2 stored. Offshore storage costs are signiﬁcantly higher than those for a reservoir in an onshore location (3.4–7.7 US$/tCO2 stored), due to the need for platforms or sub-sea facilities and higher offshore drilling costs (Allinson et al., 2003; Bock et al., 2003; IPCC, 2005). Storage in saline formations does not have any economic beneﬁts, which makes it less economically attractive than EOR, enhanced gas recovery (EGR) or ECBM production.

Storage option type, depth and geological characteristics affect the number, spacing and cost of wells (which are the major cost component), as well as the facilities cost (Bock et al., 2003; IPCC, 2005). The design basis for each of the geological and injection parameters for the aquifer storage option and the calculated number of wells are given in Table 6 (Bock et al., 2003). An increase in pressure and depth causes an increase in storage costs, in particular well and compression costs (Bock et al., 2003; IPCC, 2005). A higher reservoir pressure results in lower injectivity (not desired) but higher carbon dioxide densities (desired), and therefore a moderate pressure is optimal. In general, the permeability is the most critical parameter in determining costs. Reservoirs that are thick, shallow and have high permeability require a smaller number of wells and, therefore, present a lower storage cost (Bock et al., 2003).

Natural oil seeps and tar are widely found in the area. Using geological information from published references (Sylves- ter and Brown 1988; Harden 1997) and our own knowledge of the site, we assigned values in the SRF appropriate for the Ventura Oil Field. As shown in Fig. 2, the Ventura Oil Field ranks lower than the Rio Vista Gas Field. The SRF was also applied to a naturally leaking site for veriﬁcation purposes. Mammoth Mountain, California, is a 200,000 year-old dormant volcano with active springs, geothermal anomalies, and CO2 seepage that has killed native trees and also skiers who fell into enclosed depres- sions in the snow. For this purely academic analysis of the potential HSE effects of deliberate CO2 injection, we as- sume the area under consideration is comparable to Rio Vista and Ventura in terms of size by considering the entire Mammoth Mountain area. Using published information from (Farrar et al. 1995; Sorey et al. 1999) we ﬁlled in values and properties of the SRF spreadsheet. Many of the properties are given the lowest values because they simply do not apply at Mammoth Mountain. For example, as evidenced by the extensive seepage, we have concluded that there is no effective seal present, and therefore scored those properties with the lowest values. Other properties are not very well known and we scored them accordingly. As shown in Fig. 2 (right-hand side), the Mammoth Mountain site scored badly as expected in primary and secondary containment. The site does better on attenuation potential because it is fairly windy and the population is relatively sparse. Nevertheless, the SRF spreadsheet dem- onstrates that Mammoth Mountain would not be a good place to store anthropogenic CO2 in the subsurface.

The EU’s deployment of cross-border offshore CCS projects is regulated and facilitated within a law-based framework. The EU has long embraced the pioneering role of a global trendsetter in building up and developing CCS legal framework. In a nutshell, the EU’s CCS legal and regulatory architecture demonstrates a comprehensive, multi-layered approach to balancing environmental protection with economic incentivization for offshore CCS deployment. Central to this framework is the pioneering EU CCS Directive (EU, 2009), establishing stringent regulatory conditions for site selection, environmental impact assessments, and robust liability management throughout the CCS lifecycle. This Directive is effectively integrated with broader environmental regulatory instruments, such as the EU Environmental Impact Assessment Directive, the Industrial Emissions Directive, and the Directive on Environmental Liability, thereby ensuring a consistent environmental safeguarding framework across CCS operations. Economically, the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and the EU Innovation Fund (NER 300) provide crucial ﬁnancial stimuli, reducing economic uncertainties and fostering the development and scaling of offshore CCS technologies. The recent adoption of the EU Net Zero Industry Act Regulation (EU, 2024) signiﬁcantly advances this integrated framework, setting ambitious, legally binding targets for annual CO2 storage capacities, streamlining permitting processes, and further facilitating investment conditions. Collectively, this multifaceted and evolving regulatory architecture embodies a law-based dynamic governance strategy, uniquely designed to promote CCS deployment at scale while simultaneously safeguarding environmental integrity and achieving the EU’s overarching climate neutrality

The saline aquifer in the Pohang Basin investigated in this study is located in southeast Korea (Fig. 2.2). This aquifer was chosen as a small- scale pilot project as part of Korea’s effort to reduce emissions (Kim and Shin, 2019). The aquifer bounded with faults outside and within is highly compartmentalized, representing a closed aquifer system. Injec­ tion without pressure management in this aquifer can result in high-pressure build-up, which can reactivate pre-existing faults (Kim et al., 2018). The 3D heterogeneous geological model of the Pohang basin was adapted from previous research by Jun et al. (2019) and Kim and Shin (2019). The depth of the geological interval considered as a target for CO2 injection ranged from 613 m to 810 m. The Pohang basin has a complex structure with six faults existing within and at the boundary identified through the seismic surveys: western side faults (WF1 and WF2) and eastern side faults (EF1, EF2, EF3, and EF4) (Jun et al., 2019) (Fig. 2.3). It was assumed that exceeding the critical pressure threshold of 13 MPa may reactivate pre-existing faults. The target CO2 storage horizon has a continuous low permeable layer that separates the reservoir into upper and lower aquifers (Fig. 2.4). This layer acts as a barrier for vertical flow that is essential to the GCS operation because the CO2 plume is expected to flow upwards in the vertical direction due to buoyancy. The upper aquifer consists of suc­ cessive layers of sandstone and mudstone, while the lower aquifer consists of alternating layers of sandstone, mudstone, and conglomerate (Kim et al., 2019). 2.2.2. Genetic algorithm The GA is a nature-inspired stochastic search algorithm developed by Holland (Holland, 1992). By mimicking the natural selection and breeding process, the GA can generate high-quality solutions for opti­ mization problems. The genetic search is conducted over a population of candidates (individuals). The set of individuals forms the current gen­ eration. New individuals are produced at each iteration using GA op­ erators, such as selection, crossover, and mutation. At each iteration, individuals are evaluated based on a fitness function. Individuals with high fitness scores are more likely to be selected, reproduced, and rep­ resented in the next generation. The algorithm continues to iterate through this process until the stopping criterion is met. Fig. 2.8 shows the main stages of the GA workflow.

2.3.1. Artificial neural network McCulloch and Pitts introduced ANNs inspired by the biological neuron activity in animal brains (G´eron, 2019). ANNs are a powerful tool that can map the underlying relationship of input and output data within the boundaries of training data. One common ANN is the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) network that uses a backpropagation training algorithm in learning (G´eron, 2019). MLP is composed of one input layer, one or more hidden layers, and one output layer (Fig. 2.9). Every layer is fully connected to the next layer and has a weight (w) matrix and a bias (b) vector. The activation function gives MLP the ability to learn complex nonlinear systems. There are many activation functions to consider when training a model, such as the sigmoid logistic function, the hyperbolic tangent function, and the ReLU function. The model was trained on the training set and evaluated on the testing set to ensure that it was not overfitting to the training data. In addition, early stopping was used during the training process to prevent the model from continuing to learn from the training data after it had reached its optimal performance. Specifically, the validation loss was monitored during training and stopped the training process when the validation loss stopped improving. Moreover, L2 regularization tech­ nique was employed in the model where it adds a penalty term to the loss function that encourages the model to use smaller weights, which can help prevent the model from overfitting to the training data.

Exceeding this threshold could result in potential hazards, so it is essential to ensure that well locations are not in close proximity to fault zones. All opti­ mization models created for this investigation were subjected to the pre- screening criterion. The optimal well locations determined in the models were then evaluated to ensure that they satisfied the pre-screening criteria. were observed in the distances between the injector and the producer. The challenge in applying the pressure management well in GCS is finding the balance between increased injectivity and CO2 breakthrough time (Buscheck et al., 2012). A higher injection rate can be achieved by placing the extraction well closer to the injection well. On the other hand, if the distance is too close, it results in early CO2 breakthrough and lowers the cumulative CO2 stored. Although the CO2 breakthrough in the Base model occurred somewhat later than in the other models, the lower injection rate resulted in lower cumulative CO2 stored. On the other hand, optimal solutions obtained by Models B and C achieved a better trade-off between the increased injectivity and CO2 breakthrough time (Fig. 3.10). The models aim to sup- ply energy services at minimum global cost by simultaneously making technology investment and operating decisions, primary energy resource supply decisions, and behaviour change (by region as required). They calculate the technological conﬁguration of an energy system by minimising the net present value of all energy system costs. Linear programming bases its decisions on ‘perfect foresight’, which means that the model can ‘look ahead’ to the end of the model period to ﬁnd the least-cost energy conﬁguration over the whole period, which in this study is in 5-year time steps from 2010 to 2050. The input parameters of the MARKAL and TIMES models used were harmonized for parameters that directly impact the potential of CCS technologies (Section 2.2). Fig. 1 depicts the overall mod- elling approach of this study. We have harmonized a wide range of inputs assumptions, as well as the scenarios that all models ran (Section 2.5). Some harmonized parameters come from external sources as discussed, and others come from the regional model itself. However there is a trade-off in further harmonization efforts as due to level of detail on the policy landscape and/or in the depic- tion of behavioural change that are speciﬁc to the national models; or at the other end of the spectrum, the issues related to ﬂows of energy and emissions around the target countries (and other EU countries) that is the domain of the regional model. In striking this balance, we have tried to retain the strengths of both modelling approaches.

The port authority of Rotterdam and two partners have set out to develop an open, collaborative and long term CO2 network that facilitates transport, storage and re-use of CO2. A sketch of such a CCUS transport infrastructure network can be found in Fig. 1. The basic idea is that captured CO2 is gathered onshore at the different industry sites through a network of feeders and (a) main transport pipeline(s). After the gathering of the CO2 there are roughly two options. The gathered CO2 is either transported through a main transport pipeline towards the shore where it will be conditioned for offshore transport towards

identified storage fields close to the Rotterdam harbour industrial com- plex (see, e.g., EBN and Gasunie, 2018 for potential CO2 storage fields in the Dutch North Sea), or it will be conditioned for re-use purposes and transported through a transport pipeline to sites that use CO2 as feedstock. Here, conditioning of CO2 refers to the way in which the CO2 is ‘treated’ to make it suitable for transportation and subsequent storage or re-use. For example, CO2 may need to be compressed to a certain pressure and kept a certain temperature for offshore transport. When the CO2 is re-used, e.g., in greenhouses, the captured CO2 additionally needs to be highly purified. The conditioning mostly occurs in separate stations. Whether or not CO2 is re-used impacts the requirements on these stations in the infrastructure. The capacity of the main pipelines determine the capacity of the transport network. The blue lines in Fig. 1 represent the CO2 transport network for a CCUS hub.

The following CO2 infrastructure users are in scope for this open network. First, the heavy emitters: the large scale (petro)chemical pro- ducers that see no short term cost effective alternative to CO2 emission reduction. They benefit from a large scale CO2 infrastructure with long term storage facilities. Second, the distant emitters: heavy emitters to be found a bit further away from the Rotterdam port area, such as in the Moerdijk area or the Zeeland chemical industrial cluster (DNVGL, 2020). They have similar requirements towards a CO2 transport net- work as heavy emitters, but they would require a larger onshore transport radius of the pipelines as the identified offshore storage fields are closest to the Rotterdam industrial complex. Small emitters: small petrochemical producers that do not aim for a large transport capacity. For them investing in carbon capture technologies might become attractive because of the availability of shared CO2 transport infrastructure. Next to the emitters, there are also potential users of the captured CO2. Hydrogen producers and greenhouses: these users of CO2 also require a smaller capacity and they are not interested in offshore transport to storage facilities, but they do have some more conditioning requirements for the CO2, e.g., its purity needs to be higher than for common onshore transport purposes. Hence, there are two levels of conditioning that can be required for onshore transport: standard conditioning for onshore transportation and conditioning for re-use purposes. Table 1 gives a summary of the potential users and their heterogeneous requirements towards the CO2 transport infrastructure.

With this application in mind, Section 3 presents a general frame- work for the component-based analysis of such infrastructures and their costs, with a natural cost allocation rule as a direct result. Finally, we remark that several users in Table 1 are not yet part of the core group of interested participants, while they could benefit from the use of such a transport infrastructure. Both DNVGL (2020) and the Rotterdam port authority have sketched potential future connections to the more distant emitters and future CO2 users in their CO2 transport infras- tructure plans. The potential addition of users is a reason to look for cost allocation methods that satisfy the advantageous scaling property: adding new users to the project might raise the total construction costs, but it will not result in a cost allocation increase for any of the original users. Further, coalitional rationality ensures that there is no financial reason for any subgroup of users to split off from the group and carry on independently. Both properties will be formally defined in Section 3.3, where we also show that they are satisfied by the cost allocation rule we propose.

A systematic literature review was conducted following the guideline outlined by Fl´ avio et al. (2017), Glarou et al. (2020) and Pieroni et al. (2019), with the objective to identify and analyze articles and reports on life cycle environmental impact of CCS. The review methodology fol- lowed a systematic literature review protocol, comprising three main steps. See Fig. 1. First, the data collection (research question, source selection and study selection). Second, the data analysis (information extraction and result summarization), and third, the data reporting (dissemination of results). Two main research questions (RQ) with additional sub-questions were established to guide data collection and analysis. The full review protocol is shown in SM.1.

In respect to the research questions, specific search keywords were chosen according to four different elements (method, system, technol- ogy, and infrastructure-related keywords). The keywords were then assembled into one search string and applied to the Scopus and Web of Science (WoS) databases. A search filter was added to restrain on the publishing year (2013-2024) which is deemed a suitable timeframe considering the increase in planning and deployment of CCS projects within the past decade, language (English) and document type (e.g. open-source articles; see Table 1). The string was altered through three iterations and was considered ideal when returning sufficient hits (approximately 1000 hits) while also including five pre-selected key papers by Mendoza et al. LH open-cycle expansion refrigeration is the classic pathway for CO2 liquefaction. The LH liquefaction path is widely adopted due to its simple structure, low initial investment, and lack of additional refrig­ erant requirements. However, its single-stage coefficient of performance (COP) typically falls below 1 [60], prompting the need for performance optimization. Multi-stage throttling, pre-cooling, and high-efficiency heat exchanger design are commonly employed to improve system performance. Based on this concept, the two-stage LH has become a common variant: it first throttles and liquefies the high-pressure gas with recirculation to provide pre-cooling for the main flow, followed by a second stage of compression and throttling. This approach enhances the system's heat recovery efficiency and optimized utilization of tem­ perature differentials. Khosravi et al. [61] present that the COP of the two-stage LH cycle is about 1.9, significantly higher than that of the single-stage cycle without pre-cooling. Fig. 6 compares the single-stage and two-stage LH liquefaction pathways, highlighting how the two-stage cycle substantially enhances liquefaction efficiency through secondary compression, pre-cooling, and multi-stage throttling. Zheng et al. [62] also demonstrated through energy efficiency and cost analysis that pre-cooled LH exhibits the best overall performance among all LH var­ iants. However, these improvements are primarily based on steady-state process simulations, suggesting potential discrepancies between process-level COP and engineering-level system COP, necessitating further optimization research.

By comparing the advantages and disadvantages of the three CO2 transport methods in Table 2, it is clear that: LCO2 has become the central solution for large-scale, long-distance CCS chains due to its high transport density and energy efficiency. GCO2, with its high technical maturity (TRL 6-7) and simplified system, is suitable for short-to- medium-distance continuous pipeline transport but requires additional compression stations. SCO2, transported via hydrates or slurries, offers high safety and potential for cold energy utilization. However, its development is constrained by technical challenges such as slow hydrate nucleation rates and low heat transfer efficiency, with its TRL currently at 5-6. LTLP-LCO2 is optimal for regions with established cryogenic infrastructure and moderate-to-long distances; HPAT-GCO2 is suited for tropical ports with short offshore distances and existing LNG infra­ structure; and SCO2 remains experimental, with potential for Arctic applications. Future research should deepen in three key areas: First, establish a systematic evaluation framework for determining the appli­ cable boundaries of transport methods; Second, promote synergistic design between transport and energy recovery, particularly focusing on cold energy utilization in liquid and solid systems and its coupling with power generation and energy storage systems; Third, accelerate break­ throughs in critical technologies such as hydrate formation and stability, optimization of slurry rheological properties, and pipeline structural design. Addressing these challenges will significantly enhance the effi­ ciency and safety of CO2 transport systems, reduce costs, and provide more reliable technical assurance for the practical application of marine CCS technologies.

Fig. 1 shows the conventional BOG re-liquefaction process using a refrigerant. Inlet BOG is compressed via the BOG compressor, then cooled to ambient temperature using air or water. The BOG undergoes heat exchange with an external refrigerant of a lower temperature before expanding through a Joule–Thompson (J–T) valve. By selecting proper J–T expansion path, the temperature of the BOG can be dropped and liquefied. The refrigerant is compressed, cooled, and expanded to make low temperature via a vapor compression refrigeration cycle, as shown in Fig. 1.

Fig. 2 shows the PSO algorithm [20]. When optimization begins, a population of individuals, called particles, moves step by step across a region. Each particle updates its optimal position, and the optimal po­ sition of the population is the sum of all optimal positions experienced by the individuals. After finding the best position, it determines a new velocity for each particle. As they move, the evaluation is performed again, with each particle heading towards the best position it has found so far, while also heading towards the best positions found by other particles in the swarm. The optimal solution is obtained when the termination condition is satisfied after the iterations.
