This study suggests a new index, MGI, which is defined as an extension of the existing EEDI to assess the WtW GHG intensity of maritime transportation as shown in Fig. 3. The MGI consists of WtW GHG emissions, including WtT and TtW GHG emissions. As shown in

Fig. 3, the WtT GHG emissions include all GHG emissions generated during the production process of the used fuel, such as extraction, pro­ cessing, and transportation. The TtW process in MGI includes GHG emissions from not only the propulsion and conventional auxiliary systems (CAE), but also non-conventional auxiliary systems (NCAE) such as re-liquefaction systems in CHS. In this study, three different cases of CHS were simulated to maintain tank pressure within allowable limits during a voyage: BOG venting system (Case 1) and BOG re- liquefaction system in continuous operation (Case 2) and periodic operation (Case 3). Thus, MGI’s TtW GHG emissions include not only those from fuel combustion, but also those released directly into the atmosphere, such as those generated by the BOG venting system.

The MGI is defined as the GHG emissions from WtT and TtW pro­ cesses per transport work (multiplication of unit cargo mass (tonne) and transport distance (nm)) as shown in Eq. (7). GHG emissions are calculated according to Eqs. (8) and (9) for WtT and TtW, respectively, using the amount of fuel consumed by each system. For WtT GHG emissions assessment, the WtT GHG emission per unit energy for fuel k (GHGWtT, k) provided by FuelEU database was used, as shown in Eq. (8) [21]. To evaluate TtW GHG emissions, GHGs such as methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) generated by fuel combustion are converted into CO2 equivalent using their global warming potential (GWP), as shown in Eq. (9). Fuel consumed by each system is calculated using the power consumed as in Eq. (10).

Power consumed by main engine (ME) (PWME) and CAE (PWCAE) are calculated according to the method of original EEDI, as shown in Eqs. (11) and (12), respectively [22]. The GHG emissions of the NCAE are calculated using the average value of the simulated values over the voyage days. For re-liquefaction systems that emit GHGs due to power consumption, the average power consumption (PWRLIQ,avg) is calculated as in Eq. (13). For venting systems, the average amount of vented GHGs to the atmosphere is calculated as in Eq. (14).

As shown in Fig. 7, the re-liquefaction system is designed based on the conventional BOG re-liquefaction process with a propane refrigerant using a vapor compression cycle. The propane refrigerant is compressed and cooled (R4), and expanded via J–T valve to make low temperature vapor-liquid propane stream (R5). The excess BOG is compressed and cooled using cooling water and the stream 4 is further cooled by the propane refrigerant (R5) through the heat exchanger. Then the cooled stream 5 is expanded through the J–T valve, and the partially liquefied BOG stream is injected into the LCO2 tank.

A ship is a complex energy system with fuel supply, engine, air- conditioning, lighting and other on-board energy-consuming compo­ nents (Yuan et al., 2019). A ship is also a part of a greater life cycle energy system from building and construction, ship operation and maintenance, to end-of-life management (Nian and Yuan, 2017). The shipping system was conceived from a system producing energy (V. Nian, 2016; Wang et al., 2018) and products (V. Nian, 2016) to a system delivering services (Wang et al., 2019). As such, shipping is defined as a system for providing transport services for passenger and cargo. Based on the general system boundary conditions, a life cycle ship­ ping system has both energy and non-energy inputs, and outputs carbon emissions over the lifetime. It is assumed that the system boundary of the shipping system can be formulated from three dimensions, including the boundary between the system and its environments, the boundary between the main system and its sub-systems, and physical and temporal boundaries formatting the main system (Nian et al., 2014). In this study, the life cycle shipping system is assumed to be focused on vessels transporting LPG. Coral Alameda, recorded in Clarksons Research Shipping Intelligence Network (2022), is an LPG ship with a minimum tank temperature of −104 ◦C and a maximum tank pressure of 7 bar. The maximum tank pressure of the LPG ship recorded in Clark­ sons Research Shipping Intelligence Network (2022) can even reach 20 bar. For the liquid carbon dioxide ship, with reference to Georg Hegerland and Pande (2005), conditions close to the triple point (i.e., −56.6◦C, 5.2 bar) can reduce the shipping cost. A typical LCA study on LPG or CO2 emissions due to (for example) electricity generation would involve an LCA main system for LPG or electricity production with respective system input-output and boundary conditions. These systems usually involve the transport of materials and/or fuels to sup­ port the activities within each process/stage of the life cycle system. Using the Aspen + chemical process modelling tool, we designed and simulated the performance of amine-based CO₂ capture facilities comprising (1) CO₂ absorption/desorption columns, (2) CO₂ compres­ sion to a pressure suitable for pipeline transport, (3) CO₂ dehydration to remove residual water, (4) an integrated cogeneration plant to deliver all of the heat and power needed by the capture plant, and (5) a cooling water system (Fig. 1). By including cogeneration within the facility, our designs assume that waste heat from the existing process is unavailable to help deliver the heat needed to operate the CO₂ capture system. We note that a dedicated cogeneration plant has been built for most commercial-scale amine-based industrial CO₂ capture retrofit projects in North America, including Boundary Dam [34,49], Quest [36], and Petra Nova [37,50]. Our cogeneration system is natural gas fired, and the CO₂ emissions from this are assumed to be vented in most cases, which re­ duces the net CO₂ capture at the facility. However, we also consider one case in which the cogeneration CO2 emissions are captured (see dashed line in Fig. 1). An industrial stream targeted for CO₂ removal can be characterized by the concentration of CO₂ in the stream and the mass flow of the stream. We developed separate process simulations for target streams having CO₂ concentrations of 5 mol%, 10 mol% and 15 mol%. We designed for a CO₂ capture ratio (ψCO₂) of 95% in each case, as calculated using Eq. 1.

For each input CO₂ mass fraction, ωCO₂ we simulated capture for seven different target-stream mass flow rates, resulting in ṀCO₂,CAP values of 0.10, 0.29, 0.57, 1.15, 2.29, 3.43, and 5.70 MtCO₂/y. The predominant component in most industrial gas streams that might be targeted for CO₂ removal is nitrogen (N₂), followed by lower shares of water vapor (H₂O) and oxygen (O₂) [51,52]. For simulation purposes, we assumed target streams have H₂O and O₂ concentrations of 10 mol% and 8 mol%, respectively, and we adjust the N2 concentration to achieve the desired CO₂ concentration (Table 1). We assume target streams arrive at the capture facility at near-atmospheric pressure, as would be commonly found in industry [19], with a temperature of 50 ◦C and with trace contaminant levels that do not require removal prior to CO₂ removal. Pre-treatment required for trace contaminant removal will vary widely from facility to facility, so we have opted not to model it in a generalized way, other than to acknowledge that our assumed project contingency levels (discussed in Section 3.3) subsume the cost of such pretreatment.

A few industrial processes generate CO₂-laden streams with very high concentrations of CO₂, e.g., ammonia production and natural gas pro­ cessing plants. To represent CO₂ capture at such facilities, we developed seven additional simulations (one for each of the values of ṀCO₂,CAP noted above) for target streams with 94 mol% CO₂. CO₂ capture systems for such high-purity streams comprise only CO₂ dehydration, compres­ sion, and associated cooling water [53], so we assume the capture ratio is 100% in these cases. These simulations utilize only the gray-shaded blocks in Fig. 1. Cogeneration is not needed because high-purity target streams require very little heat supply for capture. (See SI.12). Since no cogeneration block is included, the very small parasitic heat demand in these cases is met by a natural gas boiler (venting the resulting CO₂), and electricity needs are assumed to be supplied by the grid. With CCS, CO2 is captured from industrial or energy-related sources. After capture, the CO2 is dried, cleaned and compressed. Capture locations are often not located directly at the coast. There- fore, an onshore pipeline often needs to be constructed to transport the CO2 to the coastline. At the coastline, the CO2 can be further transported with an offshore pipeline or a ship to a suitable offshore storage reservoir. CO2 pipeline transport is often proposed in the liquid (dense) phase, which is the most efﬁcient for long distances (Knoope et al., 2014). Suitable operation conditions for liquid CO2 pipeline trans- port are depicted in Fig. 1. As transporting CO2 in two phases is undesirable, pumping stations can be installed along the onshore pipeline or before the pipeline goes offshore to compensate for the pressure drop which occur in the pipeline. At the injection site a

(unmanned) platform needs to be present. The CO2 pipeline trans- port chain is shown in Fig. 2. Transporting CO2 with ships on a large scale is often proposed in the liquid form, near the triple point, because the density of the CO2 is high (Aspelund et al., 2006; ZEP, 2010; Nam et al., 2013; Roussanaly et al., 2013a). However, the CO2 ships which are currently in operation for the (food) industry use slightly lower pressures and higher temperatures (ZEP, 2010). The possible oper- ation envelop for ship transport stated in the phase diagram in Fig. 1 is based on both indicated conditions. To get the CO2 into these conditions, the CO2 has to be liqueﬁed. There are multiple ways to liquefy CO2. In this study, the compressed CO2 is lique- ﬁed by ﬁrst depressurizing the CO2 through expansion valves and, subsequently, separating the liquid CO2 from the formed gaseous CO2 by using ﬂash tanks. The gaseous CO2, which can be 20–40% of the entire CO2 ﬂow, is recompressed and recycled (Yoo et al., 2013b). CO2 capture and liquefaction is a continuous process, while ship- ping is a batch process (Roussanaly et al., 2013b). Therefore, the liqueﬁed CO2 is temporarily stored until a ship arrives (ZEP, 2010). The ship will load the liqueﬁed CO2 on the ship and sail to the injec- tion site. At the injection site, the ship unloads the CO2 as quickly as possible to a temporary storage vessel2. The CO2 is not injected directly into the reservoir because the injection process prefers to have a continuous and stable CO2 ﬂow (Roussanaly et al., 2014). Moreover, the storage reservoir cannot handle the low pressure and low temperature of the liqueﬁed CO2. Consequently, the CO2 is ﬁrst pumped and subsequently heated before the CO2 is ofﬂoaded to the injection wells (Roussanaly et al., 2014; Verme

In this study, the decision is analyzed to invest in CO2 pipeline or ship transport. Although this article focuses on the transportation chain, the capture unit and the platform are incorporated to be able to analyze the costs of the CCS chain and compare them to the CO2 price. This study excludes the costs of the industrial facility or power plant, well drilling and abandoning, and monitoring of the storage reservoir, see Fig. 2.

An investment decision in the NPV approach is based on whether the project generates a positive NPV. Required inputs for the NPV approach are the estimated costs and revenues or beneﬁts during the project duration. With respect to CCS, beneﬁts will be present in the form of less CO2 emission allowances that have to be bought. Besides calculating the NPV, the levelized costs (LC) are calculated, reﬂecting the average costs of capturing, transporting and storing 1 t of CO2 throughout the project lifetime. The NPV and the LC are calculated with Eqs. (1) and (3), respec- tively. Summation formulas are used because the utilization rate is expected to decrease and the CO2 price is expected to increase over time. Consequently, the operational expenditures and beneﬁts are not constant over time. In Table 1, the different CAPEX, OPEX and abandonment expenditures (ABEX), which are included in this

Furthermore, multiple uncertainties are assessed and many of them have a stochastic behavior. Simulation techniques are the best method for analyzing problems with these characteristics (Abdel Sabour and Dimitrakopoulos, 2011; Longstaff and Schwartz, 2001). In this study, the least-squares Monte Carlo (LSMC) approach, developed by Longstaff and Schwartz (2001), is used to value the different options and compare the pipeline and ship solutions. In this study, different uncertainties are included and modeled stochastically. This means that expectations of future values are based on the current value, but elements of randomization are present in predicting the future. Two different stochastic relations are used in this study. First, the Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM), given in Eq. (4), is used for the load factor, CO2, coal and fuel oil prices. Coal and oil prices are assumed to follow a GBM, because the mean reversion rate is rather slow (Pindyck, 1999). Also the CO2 price is assumed to follow a GBM, which is consistent with (Abadie and Chamorro, 2008; Fuss et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014; Zhu and Fan, 2011). Furthermore, the utilization rate of the coal power plant is also assumed to follow a GBM. Currently, (most) coal power plants operate on base load. However, if more renew- ables penetrate the power system over time, then base load plants have to operate with more ﬂexibility. Hence, the utilization rate would decrease over time (i.e., a negative drift). In addition, there is uncertainty in the utilization rate of the coal power plant due to variation in the generated electricity by renewables, variation in the allocation of (different types of) power plants, etc. Second, the electricity price is described with a GBM with mean reversion, see Eq. The option value of switching off the capture unit temporarily can be found by comparing the sum of the dis- counted cash ﬂows with and without the option to switch off the CO2 capture unit. For the abandoning option, the question is whether it is bet- ter to abandon or continue with the project in each period t. Note that in the ﬁnal period, the project has to be abandoned, see Eq. (7). Prior to the ﬁnal period, the value of the project is the current cash ﬂow plus the sum of the future cash ﬂow(s), see Eq. (8). The future cash ﬂows are estimated by using the simulation results from the Monte Carlo analysis and a least square regression (Longstaff and Schwartz, 2001). More speciﬁcally, the ex post realized cash ﬂows of all individual simulation paths from continuing at period t + 1 are regressed by using the values of the stochastic variables as

independent parameters at period t. After the future cash ﬂows are estimated for each period, it is evaluated, along each path for each discrete time period from time zero till the end of the project dura- tion, if abandoning is more cost-effective than continuing (Abdel Sabour and Poulin, 2006; Longstaff and Schwartz, 2001; Zhu and Fan, 2011). If the sum of the estimated future cash ﬂows is lower than the ABEX of the overall project, than it is better to abandon the project, see Eq. (9). Subsequently, the value of the project is found by discounting all resulting cash ﬂows with the risk free rate to time zero and calculating the average of the project value from all paths. For estimating the future cash ﬂows for the abandoning option, only simulation results are used for the regression exercise with a cash ﬂow of zero or lower. This gives a more accurate

approximation of the value of continuing the project and increases process efﬁciency3. Note that for each time period the actual dis- counted cash ﬂows are used rather than the conditional expected value estimated in the previous period, because this would lead to an upward bias in the option value (Longstaff and Schwartz, 2001). In this study, the regression functions are based on the ﬁrst three weighted Laguerre polynomials, see Eqs. (10)–(12), as these provide more accurate results than other polynomial relations (Areal et al., 2008; Moreno and Navas, 2003). Besides the weighted Laguerre polynomials, also cross-products of the variables are included to improve the ﬁt of the regression function. Initial analysis shows that the electricity price has very little prediction power, most proba- bly due to the strong reverse rate in the GBM with mean reversion. Hence, the electricity price is not included in the regression func- tion. Overall, this leads to the regression function shown in Eq. (13).

The design and costs of the offshore pipeline are obtained from a cost minimization model developed in a previous study (Knoope et al., 2014). The outlet pressure of the offshore pipeline is set at 7 MPa, which is assumed to be high enough for direct injec- tion (Apeland et al., 2011b). Increasing the pressure by installing pumping stations would be very expensive offshore, because a plat- form with an electricity connection is needed (IEA GHG, 2002). Consequently, if the inlet pressure of the offshore pipeline is higher than the outlet pressure of the onshore pipeline (10 MPa), a pumping station has to be installed before going offshore. The transport chain considered in this project comprises ﬁve main processes as shown in Figure 1: Liquefaction and gas conditioning, intermediate storage, loading, ship and offshore unloading. To be able to liquefy the CO2 mixture it must contain sufﬁcient amounts of CO2. CO2 sources that fulﬁl such requirements are CO2 from natural gas sweetening, ammo- nia and hydrogen production, and power plants after CO2 capturing. However, the purity and composition varies from these sources and will affect both investment and operational costs for the liquefaction process. The CO2 source is assumed to deliver CO2 at 1.1 bar and 158C. The gas is saturated with water and contains 0.3 mol% of volatile gases, 0.2 mol% of heavy hydrocarbons. Impurities inﬂuence the CO2 properties, such as density, dew point, and boiling point, and thereby the energy requirement of the transport system.

The liquid or supercritical CO2 is sub-cooled by ﬂash gas from the expansion or liquid CO2 at intermediate pressures. Subcooling will improve the process efﬁciency signiﬁ- cantly. The liquid CO2 is then expanded in one or more stages to reach the liquid product speciﬁcations. Liquid expanders can be used in order to increase the process energy efﬁciency, but is not necessarily cost-effective. The ﬂash gas from the expansion and boil-off gas from the storage tanks is sent back to the compressor train at the appropriate pressure level for re-compression. Water must be removed to avoid hydrates, freezing of water and corrosion. The solubility of water in CO2 gas decreases with higher pressure and lower temperatures. Therefore, most of the water is removed in gas scrubbers after compression and cooling (points A in Figures 3–5). The last free water is removed at a pressure between 20 and 40 bar and at a temperature close to the hydrate for- mation curve. The CO2 gas is dried to ppm level by adsorp- tion (points B in Figures 3–5). The purge gas is integrated in the process to avoid loss of CO2.

The removal of volatile components is done in a packed separation column after heat rejection close to the dew point line, (points C in Figures 3–5). At transport press- ures of 6–7 bar only small fractions of volatiles, typically 0.2–0.5 mole% can be included in the product to insure that dry ice is not formed. If more volatiles are present in the feed they must be removed. A column is used to avoid venting of large quantities of CO2 to the atmos- phere. The cooling duty in the condenser is provided by vaporization of liquid CO2 at intermediate pressure stages or from the product tank. As a rule of thumb the loss of CO2 will be equal to the amount of volatiles in the feed. Centrifugal compressors will be used for compression of CO2. The number of compressor stages will depend on inlet pressure and at what pressure heat is rejected from the CO2. C1 will most likely use a two-stage compressor as shown in Figure 3. While ﬂuctuations have a rather limited impact on shipping costs, the optimal pipeline diameter depends on the ﬂow proﬁle due to the non-linear rela- tionship between pressure drops and mass ﬂow. 4.3.1. Transport costs An important issue in any discussion of CO2 transport and car- bon capture and storage is cost. Being able to model the cost of CO2 transport and understand trends is therefore a very important aspect of selecting the optimal transport technology and lowering the total cost of CCS. Depending on capacity and distance, the two transport tech- nologies can have very different costs. For distances below the switching distances, the two costs remain similar even if ship- ping becomes more and more expensive compared to pipeline as the transport distance lessens and capacity increases, as shown in Fig. 21. On the other hand, above the switching distances, the more the distance increases and the capacity decreases, the higher becomes the discrepancy between pipeline and shipping transport costs.

This study aims to identify the optimal pressure for transport of CO2 by ship. While liquid phase transport is typically preferred due to the high density, it is possible in theory to consider a wide range of transport pressures: From the triple point (5.18 bara) to the critical pressure (73.8 bara). However, Seo et al. [39] have demonstrated that transport pressures above 20 barg are not cost-attractive due to the cost of ships in such systems. The present study thus focuses on the comparison of 7 and 15 barg as pressures for transport of CO2 by ship, which are also the most relevant [24,25,42]. It is worth noting that these are sometimes referred to as the ‘low’- and ‘medium’-pressure options, respectively. In order to properly identify the optimal conditions for transport by ship, the following steps must be accounted for in the analysis: (a) The CO2 liquefaction facility, (b) the shipping supply chain, and (c) the reconditioning facility. The system boundaries adopted in this study thus start after the CO2 capture unit and ﬁnish after the post-shipping reconditioning of the CO2, as shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Illustration of the steps of a ship-based CCS chain and the system boundaries considered in the present study.

In our base cases, we consider the transport of pure CO2, available at near ambient conditions after capture, (a) between two harbours as illustrated in Figure 1a and similarly to the Longship project [42], and (b) between a harbour and an offshore storage site as illustrated in Figure 1b. These are hereinafter referred to as base cases 1 and 2, respectively. Since the transport distances and annual volumes of CO2 being transported are key to the design and cost of the CO2 transport systems [33,34], the evaluations and comparisons of the two transport pressures will be performed for a wide range of transport distances (from 50 to 2000 km) and annual transport volumes (0.5 to 20 MtCO2/year). As several additional key parameters may impact the comparison of the 7 and 15 barg transport options, a number of different scenarios aiming to understand these impacts are investigated. • The assumption in the base cases is that CO2 is liqueﬁed directly after capture as in the Longship project. However, this may not be representative of all cases. For example, CO2 from inland emitters and industrial clusters would typically be transported at high pressure via pipeline prior to liquefaction and ship transport. In such cases, the CO2 would be expected to be available at 90 bara [18] prior to its liquefaction and shipping. This corresponds to the outlet pressure of an onshore pipeline prior to liquefaction. For this reason, two scenarios (3 and 4) seek to understand if and how

optimal transport conditions are impacted if the CO2 to be transported is available at 90 bara prior to its liquefaction. • Since the presence of impurities in the CO2 stream after capture, and possible purity constraints after liquefaction, have been shown to have an impact on CO2 transport design and costs [20,21,43], ﬁve scenarios (5 to 9) seek to understand the impact of these effects on the comparison between shipping pressures. The ﬁrst three scenarios (5 to 7) investigate the impact of different types and levels of impurities presented in Table 1. In addition, stricter purity constraints may be imposed on the CO2 after the liquefaction due to potential requirements set by the buffer storages, ships or storage. For this reason, the impact of purity constraints after CO2 liquefaction is explored, for the membrane case, through two sets of purity requirements (scenarios 8 and 9): Industrial-grade (≥99% purity) and food-grade (≥99.9% purity). • Since uncertainties exist in the investment costs of CO2 ships [40], two scenarios (10 and 11) investigate the impact of these uncertainties on the comparison of the 7 and 15 barg options. Since investment costs of 7 barg shipping are thought to be considerably lower than the ones of 15 barg shipping for a given ship capacity [40], the uncertainty scenarios will consider the possibility that the costs of building 7 barg shipping have been underestimated and that the costs of 15 barg shipping have been overestimated. • Both industrial feedback and recent research studies [40] have indicated that a ship capacity beyond 10 ktCO2/ship is not very likely to be feasible for the 15 barg option since the pressure limits the practical diameter that can be considered for the CO2 tank with current tank conﬁgurations. The modelling of the CO2 liquefaction process used in this study is based on our previous paper [47], which focused on understanding the optimal design and cost of this part of the CCS chain for various scenarios. While more details of the modelling approach can be found in the aforementioned paper, a brief summary of the liquefaction modelling is presented below. In addition, the resulting characteristics and costs of the liquefaction process are summarised in Table 3 for the considered impurity and purity constraint scenarios. Modelling of the CO2 liquefaction process is the basis for an integrated techno- economic optimisation approach minimising the costs of the CO2 liquefaction process (€/tCO2). In essence, the model is used to optimise the set of process design variables presented in Figure 2 for a pre-deﬁned set of inlet and target outlet conditions, such as temperature, pressure, and purity. Based on the results from Alabdulkarem et al. [26], the

layout of the liquefaction process employed in this work is illustrated in Figure 2, and the process itself can be organised into four groups: (1) The compression train, (2) the pre-cooler, liqueﬁer, and ﬂash tank, (3) recirculation ﬂash and re-compressor, and (4) the ammonia-based refrigeration cycle. Following the capture unit, the CO2 enters the compression train 1⃝and undergoes several stages of compression to reach a suitable liquefaction pressure. The number of compression stages is dependent on the required liquefaction pressure. Three to four stages are typical if the CO2 is available at 1 bara, but compression might also not be necessary if the CO2 is already available at high pressure, as in scenarios 3 and 4. A compression stage includes a compressor, an intercooler, and a ﬂash separator removing condensed water.After the compression train, the CO2 stream passes into an impurity removal unit 2⃝ where potential impurities are removed if required. It is cooled and condensed through a pre-cooler 3⃝and a liqueﬁer cooled by an ammonia refrigeration loop 4⃝. It is worth noting that if the stream is pure CO2 or if all the impurities are condensed at a sufﬁcient high liquefaction pressure, the stream is fully condensed and slightly sub-cooled after passing through the liqueﬁer. In scenarios that consider the presence of impurities in the inlet gas, the CO2 stream may be partially condensed in the liqueﬁer. In Section 3.1 we compare the cost of CO2 transport by pipeline and ship for increasing volumes and distances. Specific cost for transport by pipeline and by ship are compared for transport distances between 50 and 800 km and for transport volumes between 0.5 and 5.0 Million tonnes per annum (Mtpa). In Section 3.2 it is assumed that a transport hub may be developed at eight selected sites in the Nordic region. For each of the eight selected transport hubs it is calculated for what volumes (and the corresponding cost) offshore pipeline transport becomes less costly than ship transport to three selected storage sites, i.e. the so-called pipeline volumetric break-even point. Thus, the least costly transport mode from the selected hubs is defined for any combination of clusters transporting CO2 to the selected storage site. The selected transport hubs represent a relevant geographical distribution of large-scale stationary CO2 emission sources in the Nordic region. The selected storage sites used for the transport cost calculations represent the reservoir for which we have the best data available in each of the three offshore regions that are relevant for the Nordic region, i.e. Faludden with respect to storage in the Baltic Sea, Gassum with respect to storage in the Skagerrak region and Utsira with respect to storage in the North Sea. In Section 3.3 it is analyzed how the reservoir injectivity may influence the choice of reservoir. The latter is particularly important in the Nordic region if the assumed storage sites in the Baltic Sea turns out to have modest or poor storage and injection capacity as has been indicated in recent reports [8, 10]. Carbon capture and storage is a necessary mitigation strategy to avoid dangerous climate change. Extensive CO2 capture and injection into the subsurface prevents its release into the atmosphere and stores it permanently for several thousand years. In Europe, the greatest part of its carbon dioxide emissions is concentrated in the boundary areas/re­ gions of the North Sea and are a product of substantial industrial activity in the countries of the north. This study is a comprehensive analysis of 441 potential locations in the North Sea territory that can be used as carbon storage sites, cate­ gorized based on the countries of origin. These are oil and gas fields, depleted or not, and several saline aquifers, with the most common belonging to the Bunter and Brent formations. Though other studies have examined the storage capacity in specific saline aquifers and/or oil and gas fields, the absence of an inclusive study for the North Sea ter­ ritory was identified. This was the motivation for this comprehensive case study, taking into account the transient pressure response upon injection, which allows us to provide a first order estimation of storage availability. The work can be used for further development of national strategy and cost analysis pertaining to CO2 storage. The CCTS supply chains developed and analyzed in this work aim at decarbonizing the Swiss WtE sector, while delivering net-negative CO2 emissions. The CO2 is captured at the industrial sites, i.e., WtE plants, and is transported via a multi-modal network (i.e., based on several possible modes of transportation) to the storage sites, where it is permanently sequestered underground. The CCTS supply chains are represented as a network, where the nodes consist of the CO2 capture sites, CO2 storage sites and transport exchange sites, as illustrated in Fig. 1. CO2 capture sites. The thirty Swiss WtE plants emit a total of ca. 4.5 MtCO2/year, about half of which are generated from biogenic sources, thus offering an opportunity to deliver negative emissions through CCTS (VBSA, 2019; Verband der Betreiber Schweizerischer Abfallverwer­ tungsanlagen (VBSA), 2021). We consider a point-source capture tech­ nology, which consists of the standard amine-based absorption process using monoethanolamine (MEA) as solvent, with a CO2 recovery rate up to 90% (Haaf et al., 2020; Lausselet et al., 2017). Whereas determining the optimal value of the recovery rate would require the combined optimization of the CCTS supply chain and of the point-source capture unit installed at the WtE plants, as well as a broader inter-sectoral analysis, we select a 90% recovery rate based on the values achieved at large-scale industrial plants (e.g. Boundary Dam SaskPower, 2021). Furthermore, while we assume that the heat required for CO2 capture is supplied internally by the WtE plant, we consider an electric energy requirement of 25 kWh/tCO2 (Ahn et al., 2013). In general, CCS comprises three main steps: CO2 capture from large point sources, CO2 transportation and CO2 storage. CO2 capture tech- nologies can be divided into three categories as depicted in Fig. 1, namely, post-combustion capture, pre-combustion capture and oxyfuel combustion capture [12]. Compared with the other two capture tech- nologies, post-combustion capture is widely applied by the current CCS projects in operation since it is easier to implement. The captured CO2 is typically compressed at supercritical state for transportation. CO2 can be transported to the storage sites for permanent sequestration via pi- peline, truck, rail and ship. Pipeline has advantage of continuous op- erating manner in large volume transportation over the other options [13]. The potential storage sites include saline aquifers, depleted oil and gas reservoirs and deep oceans. Several CCS commercial-scale projects are currently under operation throughout the world, for ex- ample, Gorgon facility in Australia [14], Jingbian CCS project in China [15] and European CCS infrastructure [16]. The high cost of CCS infrastructure has somewhat hindered its large- scale deployment, so carbon tax approach is proposed for CO2 emission control from economic incentives. It refers that the government imposes a surcharge on GHG emission for industrial processes [17]. The objective of this work is to develop an optimization-based risk management framework to address the relationship between CCS system and carbon tax under uncertainty, aiding government and in- dustry to make optimal reduction decisions. This is of great signiﬁcance because the policy uncertainty is one of the multiple factors that impact the success of CCS. The CCS planning scheme without consideration of such uncertainty may confront high risk and cannot be realized in practical operation, which costs a lot for making such wrong decisions on CCS planning. Furthermore, there is still a lacking of quantitative models for CCS risk management, since most of the previous studies are based on qualitative approaches. The proposed risk management fra- mework can provide quantitative information into the decision on how to plan the CCS network while confront low risk level. This case study puts focus on the Northeast region of China, in- cluding Heilongjiang province, Jilin province, Liaoning province and ﬁve league cities in eastern Inner Mongolia. There are reasons to select this region as study object. First, Northeast China is a signiﬁcant heavy industries base for China, locating many facilities of power sectors and manufacturing sectors [48]. The most signiﬁcant and novel contribution of, and greatest challenge for, simCCS is constructing a realistic, efﬁcient pipeline network connecting optimized CO2 sources and reservoirs. SimCCS forms the network by optimally selecting arcs (as well as pipeline capacities) from a candidate pipeline network—a large set of potential routes to be considered as part of the optimal ﬁnal network. Currently, these candidate network data, and a research methodology to construct these data, does not exist. This absence is in part responsible for CCS infrastructure models simplifying or ignoring the pipeline network. A completely integrated CCS system, however, relies on a realistic pipeline distribution system. SimCCS generates a candidate pipeline network using a pre- optimization algorithm that extracts a vector-based network (i.e., a connected set of nodes and arcs) from a raster-based (i.e., grid cells) ‘‘cost’’ surface. The cost surface used in this paper is a 1-km raster grid covering the contiguous US (Fig. 1), and represents the estimated cost to construct a pipeline across each grid cell (MIT, 2006). Natural gas pipelines have been suggested as an analog for estimating the cost of constructing CO2 pipelines (e.g., McCoy and Rubin, 2008). The cost grid was generated by reverse-engineering the contribution of geographical features (including slope, urban areas, national/state parks, and road/rail/ river crossings) to the cost of natural gas pipeline construction in the US (MIT, 2006). Each of these geographical features is represented by a separate layer of grid cells (Fig. 1), where the value in each cell is a weight representing how much that feature multiplies the base cost of pipeline construction. CO2 source capture costs are derived from the literature cited in IPCC (2005). Published studies typically include the cost of compression to a somewhat arbitrarily determined pressure for CO2 transportation by pipeline. Compression is included in capture cost studies in order to compensate for processes that operate, and thus capture CO2, at different initial pressures. The ﬁnal pressure, however, is not uniform across previous studies so the compression costs are normalized, using the assumptions in the original study, for compression to 10 MPa. Pressurization requirements above 10 MPa are based on an estimated distance that the source’s CO2 will travel through a pipeline speciﬁcally sized for that source’s quantity of CO2. These pressurization requirements are calculated by basic representations of ﬂuid ﬂow through pipelines and the resulting pressure drop over the pipeline’s estimated distance in Eqs. 15 and 16 (Appendix). SimCCS does not simultaneously optimize and iterate pressure drops so all CO2 pressurization is assumed to occur at the source. These simplifying assumptions are necessary in order to utilize existing published cost data, but the model structure is ﬂexible enough to be able to include the ﬁxed and variable costs for pressurization/ pumping stations in the costs of the candidate pipeline arcs rather than the sources (see future work in Section 7).

Consistent with most capture cost studies, it is assumed that as much as 90% of the total amount of CO2 produced by the source can be captured. Based on this maximum limit amount of CO2 that can be captured from each source, simCCS chooses how much should be captured optimally, based on the overall costs of the integrated CCS system. Reservoir costs are also modeled with ﬁxed and variable costs, converted to present values. The ﬁxed reservoir cost includes the up-front costs of site evaluation and screening, well drilling costs, and repressurization equipment costs, if necessary. Variable cost per tonne injected depends on the ﬂow of CO2 to the reservoir and the geologic properties of the reservoir. This ﬂow rate is spread out over multiple injection wells according to the ‘‘injectivity’’ of the reservoir.2 Reservoir injectivity is calculated based on an integration of the Darcy ﬂow equation for ﬂuid ﬂow in a porous media and is determined by the geologic parameters of the reservoir (formation permeability, reservoir thickness, etc.) in Eq. A full-scale CCS deployment in Malaysia constitute a massive un- dertaking that requires substantial amount of investment and carries inherent risk. It is unrealistic to assume that the construction of nationwide CCS infrastructure can be completed all at once. To supplement the evaluation of power plant CCS feasibility in Malaysia, qualitative analysis is conducted to identify the barriers and enablers of CCS implementation. Combination of two tools is used in this analysis i.e., the SWOT and PESTEL method. SWOT method identifies the external and internal factors that affects the system by identifying its strength, weakness, opportunities, and threats. PESTEL method on the other hand identifies only external factors, however it does provide a structured framework to analyse a system from political, economic, sociocultural, technological, environment and legal aspect. This study employs a holistic approach by combining SWOT (Strengths, Weak- nesses, Opportunities, Threats) and PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) analyses to comprehensively identify both external and internal factors that can potentially impact the implementation of CCS in Malaysia’s power plants. Emergency Shutdown System. Safe operation is the most important factor in the design of the CO2 terminal. In order to protect personnel and prevent equipment damage, terminals are equipped with an emergency shutdown (ESD) system. The basic purpose of this system is to safely shut ﬂows between ship and terminal in the event of an emergency. 4. DESIGN TRADE-OFFS The CO2 terminal acts as a connecting link between the CO2 source and the sink. The objective of designing such a terminal is to ensure a reliable, economical, and safe operation while transporting CO2 in and out of the terminal. Since, the CO2 transport is always done under pressure, selection of optimum thermodynamic conditions is a key variable in the design of the CO2 terminal. The pressure at which the CO2 is liqueﬁed, stored, and shipped presents the trade-oﬀs between the capital and operating cost of the entire plant. A brief comparison is made to discuss the trade-oﬀs between CAPEX and OPEX for diﬀerent sections of the CO2 terminal. 4.1. Liquefaction Unit. The OPEX slightly increases with an increase in the operating pressure of the liquefaction unit. However, operating the liquefaction unit at a higher pressure will have lower CAPEX compared to that operating at a lower pressure. This increase in CAPEX at a low liqueﬁer pressure can be explained by the constraint of having a constant CO2 yield for the liquefaction unit that requires additional pieces of equipment. 4.2. Storage Tank. An increase in the storage pressure will lead to a higher thickness of the tank, which causes an increase in the CAPEX. However, as will be discussed in Figure 12, an increase in the storage tank pressure reduces the amount of BOG generated that can help to decrease the OPEX.

CO2 can be transported via pipelines or ships, each presenting distinct trade-offs (Holm et al., 2025). Pipelines are well suited for continuous, large-volume flows but face long lead times, complex permitting processes, and limited flexibility for cross-border applica­ tions (Rui et al., 2025). In contrast, CO2 shipping offers modularity, regional adaptability, and cost advantages, particularly for early-stage CCS networks and long-distance transport (IEAGHG, 2020; Element Energy, 2018). As CCS deployment expands geographically, the need for flexible transport solutions becomes increasingly urgent. Projections suggest that CO2 shipping demand in the Asia-Pacific region alone could exceed 100 Mt annually by 2050, necessitating over 100 dedicated carriers (S&P Global, 2024; Global CCS Institute, 2022). These forecasts position CO2 shipping not as a supplementary option, but as a central enabler of future CCS infrastructure.

To focus on the environmental impacts of the transport phase, a gate- to-gate system boundary was adopted, encompassing the process from CO2 loading to subsea injection. Upstream processes, such as CO2 cap­ ture at industrial sources, and downstream operations related to long- term geological storage were excluded. Capital goods and infrastruc­ ture construction, including shipbuilding, offshore facility construction, onboard injection equipment manufacturing, and onboard capture unit manufacturing, were also excluded from the LCA boundary. Accord­ ingly, the LCA results represent operational environmental impacts within the defined transport–injection boundary, rather than full infra­ structure life-cycle impacts. To enhance the robustness and interpretability of the eTEA results, a sensitivity analysis was conducted on key parameters. As emphasized in ISO/TS 14076, eTEA outcomes can vary significantly depending on input data and underlying assumptions, making sensitivity analysis a critical component for reliable interpretation. Transportation-related factors included transport distance, annual transport capacity, ship size, and fuel type. The analysis compared results under two conditions: (1) fixed ship size with varying transport distances, and (2) fixed annual injection volume with varying transport distances. Additionally, varia­ tions in fuel type were examined to assess trends when LCA outcomes were incorporated. The transport-distance sensitivity analysis was con­ ducted by varying the route length while keeping the main ship opera­ tion assumptions consistent with the design basis summarized in Table 1. This approach was used to isolate the first-order effect of transport distance on the MCIP. Detailed ship design constraints, including fuel tank capacity, increased fuel weight, and the resulting reduction in effective CO₂ payload, were not explicitly modeled in this screening-level analysis and should be addressed in future detailed ship design and logistics studies.

excerpt: The resilience of CO2 capture and storage are not considered in this study. We refer to resilient CCTS supply chains that are resilient in terms of CO2 transport, as illustrated in Fig. 2. A CO2 transport network can be designed to be cost-optimal only (Fig. 2a) or to be cost-optimal and resilient (Fig. 2b). In this work, we refer to the latter case simply as resilient; a resilient CO2 network is designed and operated in a way that minimizes costs while complying with a specified level of resilience (see Section 4.2). We define the nominal state as the state of a supply chain where no failure occurs (Fig. 2c and d). A cost-optimal supply chain is designed to be cost-optimal with respect to the nominal state only. In contrast, a resilient supply chain is designed to be cost-optimal when accounting for both the nominal state and all possible failure states; it features backup connections that allow it to withstand failures, but might be unused in the nominal state (Fig. 2f). When a failure occurs in a cost-optimal supply chain (Fig. 2e), e.g. a pipeline stops being available due to a corrosion damage, the amount of CO2 corresponding to the failed connection is lost to the environment. In contrast, when a failure occurs in a resilient supply chain (Fig. 2f), CO2 is re-routed towards the storage site through alternative backup connections, i.e. trucks that replace the pipeline, and is eventually sequestered underground. All transport modes mentioned above, namely truck, rail, pipeline, barge and ship, can be deployed as backup connections, with each featuring specific logistic considerations.

Finally, in investigating system resilience, we refer to the distinct concepts of risk and recovery after failure. Assuming the failure of a connection, the concept of risk refers to the state of the system imme- diately after failure (red time instant in Fig. 2f), when the connection is failed and the CO2 is not yet re-routed to a backup connection. The concept of recovery (orange time interval in Fig. 2f) refers to the state of the system during the entire time interval of interest; this includes the recovery time, which is specific for each transport mode (see Table A.1) and during which the backup connection transports the CO2 re-routed from the failed connection, as well as the post-recovery period, where the system can operate in normal conditions and the backup connection is not required anymore. For all transport modes, no lag time is considered for activating the backup system.

ASEAN is a regional grouping of ten nations in Southeast Asia, namely Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam. CO2 emission from ASEAN has been trending upwards in the last five decades (Fig. 1), especially since the 1990s. As of 2019, CO2 emission from the burning of fossil fuels and cement production in ASEAN was 1.67 Gt or 4.6% of total global CO2 emission (Our World in Data, 2021). The biggest CO2 emit­ ters in ASEAN are Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and Vietnam (Fig. 1), which are also the most populated countries. All ten ASEAN nations are signatories to the Paris Agreement, and have pledged to reduce their greenhouse gas (GHG) emission voluntarily so that the earth’s surface temperature rise is below 2◦C from pre- industry times. However, to meet the aspiration of the Paris Agree­ ment, ASEAN nations must peak their GHG emission by 2030 and ach­ ieve net-zero around 2050 (IPCC, 2019a; Lau et al., 2021a). This is a tall order , especially for many developing nations in ASEAN. Many ways have been suggested for decarbonization including increased energy efficiency, electrification, renewable energies, nuclear energy, carbon dioxide utilization, etc. (DeAngelo et al., 2021; IPCC, 2014; IPCC, 2018. It is, however, generally agreed that CCS will be a necessary part of the solution to CO2 emission reduction (Davis et al., 2018; IEA, 2021b; IPCC, 2019b; Pacala and Socolow, 2004). Without

CCS, the decarbonization will be longer and more expensive (Lau, et al. 2021a; Metz et al., 2005). Consequently, there is an urgency to imple­ ment large-scale CCS projects globally. According to the Global CCS Institute (2020), there are currently 28 large-scale CCS projects oper­ ating worldwide, storing away 41 Mtpa. More are being planned. One such project is the Northern Lights Project in Norway which will capture 0.8 Mtpa of CO2 from two industrial sources (a cement factory and a waste-to-energy plant) on the south coast of Norway (Equinor, 2019). The captured CO2 will be shipped by liquid CO2 tankers over approxi­ mately 1,000 km to Norway’s west coast, from where it will be permanently stored in supercritical state in a saline aquifer at 2600 m below the sea bed. There are plans to expand the amount stored to 5 Mtpa by accepting CO2 from other European countries. There is increasing interest on CCS projects in ASEAN (IEA, 2021a). One CCS hub is proposed in East Java, Indonesia (ERIA, 2021). In addition, there is a proposal to ship CO2 captured from SE Asia to Australia for storage (Zhang, 2020). However, from Singapore’s perspective, East Java and especially Australia are rather far away for CO2 storage. Locations of past and planned CCS pilots in the study area are shown in Fig. 2. Water-alternating-gas (containing more than 50% of CO2) injection was applied in the Dulang oil field in the Malay Basin using six wells since November of 2002. Unfortunately, the pilot was suspended due to mechanical problems with the compressor (Kechut et al., 2001; Samsudin et al., 2005; Hamdan et al., 2005). There are plans for CO2 storage pilots in the Bujang, Inas, and Sepat gas fields in the

Malay Basin in the next five years (Petronas, 2020). A geological carbon storage project in the Kaliberau gas field in South Sumatra is also planned (Koning et al., 2021). In this paper, we explore the feasibility of a cross-border CCS project in ASEAN with Singapore as one of the sources of anthropogenic CO2. We estimate stationary CO2 sources and sinks within 1,000 km from Singapore. Stationary CO2 sources are power plants, refineries, cement factories and steel and iron mills. Potential CO2 sinks are oil and gas reservoirs and saline aquifers in Malaysia and Indonesia (Robinson, 1985; Murphy et al., 2005; Zahirovic et al., 2014; Purwanto et al. 2016; Doust, 2017). Within ASEAN, many oil reservoirs are in the mature development stage while most gas reservoirs are still in the early depletion stage (Riva, 1983; Seong and Hong, 1995; Todd et al., 1997; Bishop, 2002; Selamat et al., 2008; Hall, 2009; Yuwono et al., 2012; Iskandar et al., 2013). The study area consists of eight sedimentary ba­ sins (Table 1). They are the North Sumatra, Central Sumatra, South Sumatra, Northwest Java, Penyu, Malay, West Natuna and East Natuna basins (Fig. 3).

The target system in this study is a port-to-port CO2 transport chain, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The temperature and pressure at Points 2 and 4 in the reliquefaction cycle play significant roles in determining system efficiency. Fig. 4 show the variation in temperatures and pressures at Points 2 and 4 for discharge temperature limits of 100 ◦C, 110 ◦C, and 120 ◦C. As the seawater temperature rises from 15 ◦C to 35 ◦C, the temperatures and pressures at Points 2 and 4 increase until the discharge temperature limit is reached. Once the limit, particularly at 100 ◦C, is reached, a bottle­ neck occurs in the system. This condition restricts the ability of the compressor to further increase the pressure, leading to a reduction in pressure at Point 4. This phenomenon occurs because the compression process is isentropic. As the seawater temperature rises, the cooled CO2 temperature at Point 3 also increases before entering the second compressor. With this elevated temperature, the isentropic compression process results in a lower final pressure when reaching the discharge temperature limit, causing the pressure at Point 4 to drop. For instance, at the 100 ◦C discharge limit, the system reaches this temperature when the seawater temperature is around 30 ◦C. Beyond this point, as the seawater temperature continues to increase, the discharge pressure of the compressor decreases. A similar effect is observed at the 110 ◦C limit,

Fig. 5 illustrates the relationship between the vapor ratio and the overall mass flow rate as the seawater temperature increases from 15 ◦C to 35 ◦C for different discharge temperature limits (100 ◦C, 110 ◦C, and 120 ◦C). As the seawater temperature rises, the vapor ratio steadily in­ creases, which subsequently leads to a rise in the mass flow rate through the system. The vapor ratio at the separator increases significantly as the system reaches its discharge temperature limit prematurely, especially at the 100 ◦C limit. This effect is more pronounced at higher seawater temperatures. For instance, at a seawater temperature of 35 ◦C and a discharge temperature limit of 100 ◦C, the vapor ratio reaches approx­ imately 0.82, resulting in a sharp rise in the mass flow rate, which be­ comes approximately 3.04 times greater than the value at a seawater temperature of 15 ◦C. This occurs because reaching the discharge limit prevents Compressor 2 from sufficiently increasing the pressure, leading to a considerable increase in the vapor ratio. In contrast, for discharge temperature limits of 110 ◦C and 120 ◦C, the vapor ratios and corre­ sponding mass flow rates show a comparatively gradual increase, highlighting the importance of selecting discharge temperature limits to control vapor ratios and overall mass flow rate effectively.

As seawater temperature increases, the compressor work for both Stage 1 and Stage 2 also increases consistently across all discharge temperature limits, as shown in Fig. 6. The primary reason for this trend is that compressor work is directly related to the product of mass flow and the enthalpy difference between the inlet and outlet.
